suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Compare evidence from the story with historical information about the rest cure and Gilman's essay explaining why she wrote the story. How does each source contribute to interpretation?

suggestedTexts.title: Why I Wrote The Yellow Wallpaper
suggestedTexts.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate an author's retrospective account as a primary source for literary interpretation.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Explain how Gilman's account clarifies the story's historical context and purpose. What interpretive questions remain even after reading the author's explanation?

suggestedTexts.title: Historical newspaper coverage of the Titanic disaster
suggestedTexts.author: Various contemporary journalists
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare early reporting, incomplete information, and later historical verification.
suggestedTexts.access: Library of Congress Chronicling America collection
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; historical newspaper formatting may require support.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Why did some early reports about the Titanic give readers inaccurate information?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Compare newspaper accounts published immediately after the disaster with later reporting. Identify which claims changed as more reliable evidence became available.

suggestedTexts.title: Teen Social Media and Technology reports
suggestedTexts.author: Pew Research Center
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate sample characteristics, survey questions, methodology, publication dates, and the limits of statistical claims.
suggestedTexts.access: Pew Research Center website
suggestedTexts.readingTime: 15–25 minutes for a selected report and methodology section
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; support graph and percentage interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Identify what the survey actually measures. Compare the report's findings with a news headline describing the research. Does the headline accurately represent the evidence?

suggestedTexts.title: Youth Risk Behavior Survey reports
suggestedTexts.author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
suggestedTexts.purpose: Practice locating original datasets, evaluating research scope, and interpreting findings accurately.
suggestedTexts.access: CDC website
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; select age-appropriate topics and provide statistical support.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Identify the population, year, and variables represented in a selected finding. Explain which conclusions the evidence supports and which conclusions would go beyond the data.

suggestedTexts.title: Climate Change: Evidence and Causes
suggestedTexts.author: National Academy of Sciences and the Royal Society
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate scientific authority, supporting evidence, and explanations of common misconceptions.
suggestedTexts.access: National Academies and Royal Society websites
suggestedTexts.readingTime: 15–25 minutes for selected questions and answers
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Select one scientific claim and trace the evidence used to support it. Compare the explanation with a popular media account of the same issue.

suggestedTexts.title: The MLA Style Center
suggestedTexts.author: Modern Language Association
suggestedTexts.purpose: Apply current MLA documentation principles to authentic research materials.
suggestedTexts.access: MLA Style Center website
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Use the MLA core elements to construct citations for a book, journal article, and website. Explain how each in-text citation directs the reader to its Works Cited entry.

suggestedTexts.title: Civic Online Reasoning instructional materials
suggestedTexts.author: Digital Inquiry Group
suggestedTexts.purpose: Practice lateral reading, source verification, and evidence-based evaluation of online information.
suggestedTexts.access: Digital Inquiry Group website; registration or access conditions may apply.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Investigate who is behind an unfamiliar website before evaluating its individual claims. Record which independent sources help establish credibility.

differentiation.title: Source Type Sorting Lab
differentiation.activity: Students sort sample source cards into primary, secondary, tertiary, scholarly, popular, and governmental categories. They then match each source to a research question for which it would be useful.
scaffolds: Provide color-coded categories.
Model the classification of two sources.
Allow students to explain their choices orally before writing.
Clarify that a source may belong to more than one category.
differentiation.success: Students accurately classify most sources and explain why at least two sources are appropriate for particular questions.

differentiation.title: Search Terms That Work
differentiation.activity: Students begin with an overly broad question about teenage sleep. They identify its major concepts, generate synonyms, and use guided database searches to narrow results.
scaffolds: Provide a keyword bank.
Model AND and OR with a visual diagram.
Use a partially completed search organizer.
Provide screenshots of database filters when needed.
differentiation.success: Students locate at least two relevant sources and explain how a revised search improved their results.

differentiation.title: Credible or Relevant?
differentiation.activity: Students evaluate four sources for a question about high school start times. They place each source on a two-axis chart representing credibility and relevance.
scaffolds: Define credibility and relevance separately.
Provide guiding questions about expertise and topic alignment.
Complete one example together.
differentiation.success: Students explain why a credible source may still be irrelevant and why a relevant source may still require verification.

differentiation.title: Citation Matching
differentiation.activity: Students match quotations and paraphrases with their correct MLA in-text citations and Works Cited entries.
scaffolds: Highlight matching author names and titles.
Begin with sources containing page numbers.
Introduce sources without page numbers after initial practice.
Provide immediate corrective feedback.
differentiation.success: Students correctly connect evidence, in-text citations, and Works Cited entries.

differentiation.title: Paraphrase Without Patchwriting
differentiation.activity: Students read a short informational passage, identify its central idea, set the original aside, and explain the idea in their own words. They compare their paraphrase with the original for accuracy and independence of wording.
materials: Examples of effective and ineffective paraphrases
scaffolds: Allow oral rehearsal.
Provide vocabulary explanations.
Model changing sentence structure rather than replacing isolated words.
Use a citation sentence frame.
differentiation.success: Students produce an accurate paraphrase with substantially original wording and appropriate attribution.

differentiation.title: Academic Database Scavenger Hunt
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a shared topic using an academic database. They locate a scholarly article, a professionally edited news or magazine article, and a relevant reference source. Students record search terms, filters, publication information, and reasons for selecting each result.
materials: Academic database access through the school library or GALILEO
scaffolds: Provide a list of approved research topics.
Model reading abstracts and subject headings.
Provide an example completed research log.
differentiation.success: Students independently locate three appropriate sources and explain how each contributes differently to the research question.

differentiation.title: Lateral Reading Investigation
differentiation.activity: Students evaluate an unfamiliar website by investigating its author, publisher, funding, and reputation through independent sources. They distinguish the site's self-description from externally verifiable information.
scaffolds: Model opening additional tabs before reading deeply.
Provide questions about organizational ownership and expertise.
Remind students that domain endings alone do not establish credibility.
differentiation.success: Students support a nuanced credibility judgment with independently verified evidence.

differentiation.title: Follow the Statistic
differentiation.activity: Students select a statistic from a news article or infographic and trace it to the original research report or dataset. They compare the original population, date, wording, and findings with the secondary presentation.
scaffolds: Model following hyperlinks and references.
Provide a checklist for population, sample, date, and measured variable.
Use a teacher-selected statistic with an accessible original source.
differentiation.success: Students accurately identify the original evidence and explain whether the secondary presentation preserves its meaning.

differentiation.title: When Credible Sources Disagree
differentiation.activity: Students compare two credible sources that reach different conclusions about a shared topic. They examine definitions, evidence, research methods, publication dates, populations, and limitations before developing a qualified conclusion.
scaffolds: Provide annotated abstracts.
Model distinguishing disagreement about facts from disagreement about interpretation.
Offer sentence frames for qualified conclusions.
differentiation.success: Students identify at least two plausible reasons for disagreement and develop a conclusion that accurately represents both sources.

differentiation.title: Bias Without Dismissal
differentiation.activity: Students compare coverage of a shared issue from sources with different institutional or editorial perspectives. They identify differences in evidence selection, framing, terminology, and omissions, then evaluate specific claims independently.
scaffolds: Distinguish perspective from factual inaccuracy.
Model evaluating individual claims.
Require students to identify accurate information in more than one source.
differentiation.success: Students explain how perspective shapes presentation without assuming that bias automatically makes all information false.

differentiation.title: Evidence Ranking Workshop
differentiation.activity: Students receive a research question and a collection of possible evidence. They rank the evidence according to relevance, credibility, specificity, and explanatory value, then defend their selections in a short analytical response.
scaffolds: Provide a worked example.
Allow collaborative ranking before independent writing.
Encourage students to identify limitations in even their strongest evidence.
differentiation.success: Students select evidence based on defensible criteria and explain why weaker evidence is less useful.

differentiation.title: Literary Interpretation with Research
differentiation.activity: Students develop an interpretation of a short story using direct textual evidence and one relevant historical or scholarly source. They distinguish what the primary text demonstrates from what contextual research helps explain.
materials: Academic database or curated secondary sources
scaffolds: Provide sample interpretive questions.
Model integrating literary and contextual evidence.
Provide a paragraph structure emphasizing claim, evidence, and reasoning.
differentiation.success: Students produce a defensible literary interpretation supported by accurate textual evidence, relevant secondary research, and MLA documentation.

differentiation.title: MLA Citation Clinic
differentiation.activity: Students construct Works Cited entries for a print book, a journal article accessed through a database, and a website. They then create corresponding in-text citations and audit the relationship between each citation and its entry.
scaffolds: Provide a core-elements organizer.
Model containers using a journal article.
Explain how to handle unavailable publication information.
Allow citation generators as drafting aids only when students verify their output.
differentiation.success: Students create identifiable, substantially correct MLA entries and corresponding in-text citations without inventing missing information.

differentiation.title: Investigate a Widely Repeated Claim
differentiation.activity: Students select a widely circulated historical, scientific, cultural, or media claim and investigate its origin. They trace the claim through multiple publications, distinguish independent confirmation from repetition, and produce an evidence-based verification report.
scaffolds: Require teacher approval of claims.
Provide checkpoints for original-source identification.
Encourage students to acknowledge unresolved questions.
differentiation.success: Students reconstruct the claim's source history, evaluate independent evidence, and communicate a qualified conclusion with accurate citations.

differentiation.title: Research Methods Detective
differentiation.activity: Students compare two studies investigating related questions. They evaluate sample selection, variables, data collection, research design, and limitations, then explain how methodological differences affect the conclusions.
scaffolds: Select studies with accessible methods sections.
Provide background on correlation and causation.
Allow students to consult disciplinary experts or reference materials.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate the strength and limitations of each study without overstating what the findings establish.

differentiation.title: Historical Reporting Reconstruction
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a historical event through contemporary newspaper coverage, primary documents, and later historical scholarship. They create a timeline showing how public understanding changed as new evidence became available.
scaffolds: Provide a shortlist of researchable events.
Model interpreting historical newspaper language and layout.
Require students to distinguish what was known at the time from later discoveries.
differentiation.success: Students explain changes in historical interpretation using multiple independently evaluated sources and MLA citations.

differentiation.title: The Source Portfolio
differentiation.activity: Students develop an annotated research portfolio containing six sources representing different source types and perspectives. For each source, they explain its relevance, credibility, limitations, and relationship to other sources. They conclude with a synthesis identifying agreements, tensions, and unanswered questions.
scaffolds: Require a focused research question.
Provide an example analytical annotation.
Schedule individual research conferences.
differentiation.success: Students curate a purposeful collection of sources and demonstrate that they understand how the sources work together to address a complex question.

differentiation.title: AI Citation and Claim Audit
differentiation.activity: Students examine a teacher-provided AI-generated research response containing a mixture of accurate claims, unsupported statements, and potentially fabricated citations. They verify each claim and citation using academic databases, library catalogs, and original publications.
scaffolds: Use a prepared response rather than requiring individual AI accounts.
Model checking whether an article actually exists.
Require verification against original sources rather than another AI response.
Distinguish unsupported claims from demonstrably false claims.
differentiation.success: Students identify which claims and citations can be verified, correct inaccuracies, and explain why generated text is not a substitute for documented research.

questions.prompt: A student is researching whether later school start times affect high school students' sleep. Which source would provide the strongest starting point for evaluating the relationship?
options: A mattress company's advertisement explaining the importance of sleep
A peer-reviewed study measuring sleep among high school students before and after a schedule change
An anonymous social media post about being tired at school
A general encyclopedia entry about the history of education
questions.answer: A peer-reviewed study measuring sleep among high school students before and after a schedule change
questions.rationale: The study directly addresses the research question and provides systematic evidence from the relevant population.

questions.prompt: Which search would most effectively locate research about social media use and adolescent sleep?
options: Teenagers
Social media OR sleep OR adolescents
Social media AND sleep AND adolescents
Everything about phones
questions.answer: Social media AND sleep AND adolescents
questions.rationale: AND combines the major concepts so that results are more likely to address their relationship.

questions.prompt: A database search for artificial intelligence produces thousands of results. What is the most effective next step for a student investigating AI-generated misinformation?
options: Select the first result without reading its description
Limit the search to relevant concepts such as generative AI and misinformation
Remove all search terms
Use only articles containing the word technology
questions.answer: Limit the search to relevant concepts such as generative AI and misinformation
questions.rationale: A focused search improves relevance by identifying the specific relationship being investigated.

questions.prompt: Which action best demonstrates lateral reading?
options: Reading every page of an unfamiliar website
Trusting a website because it looks professional
Opening independent sources to investigate the website's publisher and reputation
Checking whether the website uses complete sentences
questions.answer: Opening independent sources to investigate the website's publisher and reputation
questions.rationale: Lateral reading involves investigating a source through information outside the source itself.

questions.prompt: A medical research article is credible but examines adults over age sixty. A student is investigating the health experiences of teenagers. What is the primary limitation of the article for this project?
options: It is necessarily inaccurate.
It may have limited relevance to the population being investigated.
It cannot be cited in MLA format.
It is automatically biased because it concerns adults.
questions.answer: It may have limited relevance to the population being investigated.
questions.rationale: Credibility and relevance are separate considerations. Research on one population may not apply directly to another.

questions.prompt: Which source would be a primary source for studying public reactions to the sinking of the Titanic?
options: A newspaper article published in April 1912
A modern encyclopedia entry about the Titanic
A twenty-first-century historian's analysis
A contemporary textbook chapter summarizing the disaster
questions.answer: A newspaper article published in April 1912
questions.rationale: Contemporary reporting provides direct historical evidence of how the event was presented at the time.

questions.prompt: Five news websites report the same statistic, but all five cite one original study. What should a researcher conclude?
options: The statistic has been independently confirmed five times.
The statistic must be false because it appears repeatedly.
The reports may represent repeated coverage of one source rather than independent corroboration.
The statistic no longer requires citation.
questions.answer: The reports may represent repeated coverage of one source rather than independent corroboration.
questions.rationale: Multiple publications repeating one study do not constitute multiple independent investigations.

questions.prompt: A company publishes research suggesting its own product improves student achievement. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Reject the findings automatically.
Accept the findings because the company understands its product.
Examine the methodology, funding, limitations, and independent research before evaluating the claim.
Assume the findings are unbiased because they contain statistics.
questions.answer: Examine the methodology, funding, limitations, and independent research before evaluating the claim.
questions.rationale: A potential conflict of interest warrants investigation but does not independently establish that the findings are false.

questions.prompt: Two credible studies reach different conclusions about the relationship between homework and academic achievement. What should a student investigate first?
options: Which study has the longer title
Whether the studies used different populations, definitions, methods, or time periods
Which conclusion agrees with the student's personal opinion
Whether one study has more colorful charts
questions.answer: Whether the studies used different populations, definitions, methods, or time periods
questions.rationale: Differences in research design and scope may explain apparently conflicting findings.

questions.prompt: A survey finds that students who sleep fewer hours report more stress. Which conclusion is most justified by this information alone?
options: Sleeping fewer hours causes all student stress.
Stress always causes students to sleep fewer hours.
The survey identifies an association between sleep duration and reported stress.
Students who sleep longer never experience stress.
questions.answer: The survey identifies an association between sleep duration and reported stress.
questions.rationale: An observed correlation does not independently establish causation.

questions.prompt: Which information is most important when evaluating whether a statistic from a 2015 study accurately describes current social media use?
options: The font used in the original report
The number of photographs in the report
Whether more recent evidence indicates that usage patterns have changed
Whether the report's title is interesting
questions.answer: Whether more recent evidence indicates that usage patterns have changed
questions.rationale: Currency is especially important for rapidly changing subjects.

questions.prompt: A headline states that a new study proves homework is harmful. The original study reports a limited association between excessive homework and stress in one student population. What is the main problem with the headline?
options: It uses too few words.
It exaggerates the scope and certainty of the original findings.
It refers to a scholarly study.
It discusses a controversial topic.
questions.answer: It exaggerates the scope and certainty of the original findings.
questions.rationale: The headline transforms a limited association into a broad causal conclusion that the study does not establish.

questions.prompt: Which action most directly verifies whether a quotation has been taken out of context?
options: Counting how many websites repeat the quotation
Reading the original passage or recording and examining the surrounding discussion
Checking whether the quotation is grammatically correct
Selecting the interpretation that sounds most convincing
questions.answer: Reading the original passage or recording and examining the surrounding discussion
questions.rationale: The original context is necessary to determine whether the quotation accurately represents the speaker's meaning.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the purpose of an academic article's abstract?
options: It provides a brief overview that helps readers evaluate the article's potential relevance.
It replaces the complete article for every research purpose.
It proves that every conclusion in the article is correct.
It lists all articles available in the database.
questions.answer: It provides a brief overview that helps readers evaluate the article's potential relevance.
questions.rationale: An abstract supports initial source selection, but detailed evaluation may require reading the complete article.

questions.prompt: Which source is most appropriate for establishing what a particular historical law actually stated?
options: A modern social media discussion of the law
The original text of the law
An unrelated political speech
A fictional story inspired by the period
questions.answer: The original text of the law
questions.rationale: The original legal document provides direct evidence of its wording.

questions.prompt: A student quotes a passage from page 87 of a book by Maria Chen. Which MLA parenthetical citation is correct if the author's name does not appear in the sentence?
options: (Maria Chen, p. 87)
(Chen 87)
(87, Chen)
questions.answer: (Chen 87)
questions.rationale: MLA generally uses the author's surname and the relevant page number without a comma or p. in this situation.

questions.prompt: A student writes, Chen argues that the character's isolation reflects broader social expectations. The information appears on page 87 of Chen's book. Which parenthetical citation is appropriate?
options: (Chen 87)
(Maria Chen, 87)
(p. 87, Chen)
questions.rationale: When the author's name appears in the sentence, the parenthetical citation generally supplies the page number without repeating the name.

questions.prompt: A student paraphrases an online article by Jordan Rivera that has no page numbers. The author's name does not appear in the sentence. Which citation is generally appropriate?
options: (Rivera)
(Rivera 1)
(Rivera, no page)
No citation is needed because the source is online.
questions.answer: (Rivera)
questions.rationale: MLA does not require invented page numbers for unpaginated sources. The author reference connects the information to the Works Cited entry.

questions.prompt: Which statement about paraphrasing is correct?
options: A paraphrase never requires a citation.
A paraphrase should preserve the source's meaning while using substantially original language and appropriate attribution.
Changing three words in a source sentence always creates an acceptable paraphrase.
A paraphrase must be longer than the original passage.
questions.answer: A paraphrase should preserve the source's meaning while using substantially original language and appropriate attribution.
questions.rationale: Paraphrasing requires accurate restatement, independent wording and structure, and acknowledgment of the source.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an MLA Works Cited entry?
options: To make an essay appear longer
To provide enough identifying information for readers to locate the cited source
To prove that the source is unbiased
To replace the writer's explanation of evidence
questions.answer: To provide enough identifying information for readers to locate the cited source
questions.rationale: Works Cited entries support transparency, attribution, and source retrieval.

questions.prompt: Which item would generally be the container for a scholarly article?
options: The article's first sentence
The journal in which the article appears
The author's surname
The article's conclusion
questions.answer: The journal in which the article appears
questions.rationale: A container is a larger work that contains the source being cited.

questions.prompt: A citation generator produces an entry with a publication date that does not match the original article. What should the student do?
options: Keep the generated entry because citation generators are always accurate.
Delete the publication date without checking MLA guidance.
Verify the source information and correct the entry.
Change the date in the original article.
questions.answer: Verify the source information and correct the entry.
questions.rationale: Citation generators are tools that require human verification.

questions.prompt: An AI-generated research response lists a journal article that cannot be located through the journal website, academic databases, or library catalogs. What is the most responsible action?
options: Cite the article because its title sounds scholarly.
Invent missing publication information.
Treat the citation as unverified and locate a real source before using the claim.
Ask another AI tool whether the article sounds authentic.
questions.answer: Treat the citation as unverified and locate a real source before using the claim.
questions.rationale: Generated citations may be inaccurate or fabricated and must be independently verified.

questions.prompt: Which response best demonstrates synthesis?
options: Listing one summary after another without explaining their relationships
Copying the conclusion of the longest source
Explaining how findings from several sources agree, conflict, or complement one another in relation to a research question
Using only sources that support an initial opinion
questions.answer: Explaining how findings from several sources agree, conflict, or complement one another in relation to a research question
questions.rationale: Synthesis connects evidence across sources to develop a more complete understanding.

questions.prompt: A student finds a source that challenges the central argument of an essay. What is the strongest research practice?
options: Ignore the source because it complicates the argument.
Evaluate the source and revise or qualify the argument if its evidence is persuasive.
Remove all sources that disagree.
Assume the source is biased without investigating it.
questions.answer: Evaluate the source and revise or qualify the argument if its evidence is persuasive.
questions.rationale: Responsible research requires openness to credible evidence that challenges initial assumptions.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between credibility and relevance. Provide an example of a credible source that would not be especially relevant to a specific research question.
questions.answer: Responses should explain that credibility concerns trustworthiness, expertise, and evidence, while relevance concerns the source's relationship to a particular question. For example, a credible study about adult workplace productivity may have limited relevance to a question about elementary school reading instruction.
questions.rationale: Students must evaluate sources according to multiple independent criteria.

questions.prompt: A website identifies itself as an independent educational research organization. Describe three actions you could take to verify that description.
questions.answer: Responses may include investigating the organization's ownership and funding, checking the qualifications of its researchers, consulting independent reporting or institutional records, and examining whether its publications provide transparent methods and supporting evidence.
questions.rationale: Students should use independent verification rather than relying exclusively on a source's self-description.

questions.prompt: Explain why a source with an identifiable bias may still be useful in research.
questions.answer: A source with a particular perspective may provide accurate evidence, firsthand experience, or valuable insight into how an issue is understood. Researchers should identify its perspective, evaluate specific claims, and compare its information with other sources.
questions.rationale: The task requires nuanced evaluation rather than treating bias as an automatic reason for rejection.

questions.prompt: Two studies about adolescent screen time report different findings. Identify three possible reasons for the disagreement.
questions.answer: Possible reasons include different definitions of screen time, different age groups or populations, different research methods, different time periods, different sample sizes, and different outcomes being measured.
questions.rationale: Students should investigate methodological and contextual differences before deciding that one source must be incorrect.

questions.prompt: Explain why finding a quotation on several websites does not necessarily establish that the quotation is authentic.
questions.answer: The websites may have copied the quotation from the same inaccurate source. Authenticity requires tracing the quotation to an original document, recording, reliable transcript, or other independently verified evidence.
questions.rationale: The question assesses understanding of provenance and independent corroboration.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate whether a viral infographic accurately represents the research it cites.
questions.answer: Identify the original report or dataset, verify the statistic, examine the population and date, compare the infographic's wording and scale with the original findings, and determine whether important qualifications or limitations have been omitted.
questions.rationale: Students should evaluate the accuracy and presentation of information rather than simply accepting a visual source.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a summary and a paraphrase. Why do both generally require attribution when they present another author's ideas?
questions.answer: A summary condenses a larger text into its main ideas, while a paraphrase restates a more specific idea in original language. Both require attribution because the underlying ideas or information originate with another source.
questions.rationale: The task assesses understanding of source use and intellectual accountability.

questions.prompt: A student cites an article as (Patel 16), but the Works Cited page contains no entry beginning with Patel. Explain the problem and how to correct it.
questions.answer: The reader cannot reliably identify the source corresponding to the in-text citation. The student should add or correct the Works Cited entry and ensure that its identifying element matches the citation.
questions.rationale: In-text citations and Works Cited entries function as a connected documentation system.

questions.prompt: A student discovers that a source previously used in an essay contains a factual error. What should the student do?
questions.answer: The student should verify the error, locate more reliable evidence, revise any affected claims, correct or replace the citation as appropriate, and reconsider conclusions that depended on the inaccurate information.
questions.rationale: Research writing should be revised when the quality or accuracy of evidence changes.

questions.prompt: Compare two sources that address the same research question but reach different conclusions. Evaluate each source's credibility, relevance, evidence, methodology, and limitations. Explain possible reasons for the disagreement and develop a qualified conclusion supported by both sources.
questions.answer: A successful response identifies the shared question, accurately represents each source, evaluates the evidence and methods, explains meaningful similarities and differences, acknowledges limitations, and develops a conclusion supported by appropriate MLA citations.
questions.rationale: This task integrates source evaluation, comparison, synthesis, and documentation.

questions.prompt: Develop a literary interpretation of a selected short story using at least two passages from the primary text and one credible secondary source. Explain how the secondary source supports, challenges, or complicates your interpretation. Include MLA in-text citations and a Works Cited page.
questions.answer: A successful response presents a defensible interpretation, selects relevant textual evidence, evaluates the secondary source, explains the relationship between primary and secondary evidence, and documents all sources accurately.
questions.rationale: The task applies research and citation skills to inferential literary analysis.

questions.prompt: Investigate a widely circulated claim by locating its original source and at least two additional sources that provide independent evidence or meaningful context. Write a verification report explaining whether the claim is accurate, misleading, unsupported, or unresolved.
questions.answer: A successful report identifies the precise claim, traces its provenance, evaluates independent evidence, distinguishes verified facts from interpretations, acknowledges uncertainty when appropriate, and includes accurate MLA documentation.
questions.rationale: The task assesses advanced source evaluation, corroboration, and responsible communication of findings.

questions.prompt: Create an annotated bibliography for a research question using four credible sources representing at least two different source types. For each source, explain its relevance, authority, evidence, perspective, and limitations. Conclude by identifying how the sources complement or challenge one another.
questions.answer: A successful bibliography contains accurate MLA entries, analytical rather than merely descriptive annotations, purposeful source selection, and a concluding synthesis that explains relationships among the sources.
questions.rationale: The task assesses the student's ability to curate a useful research collection rather than simply accumulate citations.

evidence: A research log showing initial search terms, revised searches, filters, and selected results.
A source portfolio containing credible and relevant print and digital materials, including academic database results.
An explanation of why particular sources were selected and why others were rejected.
A source evaluation chart distinguishing credibility, relevance, validity, accuracy, and currency.
A lateral reading investigation supported by independently verified information.
A claim-verification report tracing a quotation, statistic, image, or assertion to its original context.
A comparison of conflicting sources that identifies differences in evidence, methods, definitions, or perspectives.
An analysis explaining how author bias influences the selection or presentation of information.
An evidence-ranking activity supported by clear criteria and reasoning.
An annotated bibliography that evaluates sources rather than merely summarizing them.
A synthesis matrix organizing information according to claims, agreements, disagreements, and limitations.
A literary analysis incorporating primary textual evidence and relevant secondary research.
A research paragraph that accurately integrates quotations, paraphrases, or summaries.
A Works Cited page containing identifiable entries for cited sources.
An MLA citation audit demonstrating correspondence between in-text citations and Works Cited entries.
A revised research response showing corrections to unsupported claims, inaccurate attribution, or weak evidence.
A reflection explaining how newly discovered evidence changed or qualified an initial conclusion.

Teach students to identify the kind of evidence a question requires before selecting a source or search platform.
Collaborate with the school librarian to model academic database searching, library catalog use, and access to credible digital collections.
Use school-provided databases, including appropriate GALILEO resources, to demonstrate the differences among scholarly journals, newspapers, magazines, and reference publications.
Model translating a research question into searchable concepts, synonyms, and subject terms.
Teach Boolean operators through authentic searches rather than isolated vocabulary memorization.
Demonstrate how publication date, subject, source type, and peer-review filters change search results.
Explain that database inclusion and peer-review status are useful indicators but do not eliminate the need to evaluate individual sources.
Teach students to use abstracts for initial screening while consulting full texts when evaluating detailed claims or methods.
Model the difference between a source's general credibility and its suitability for a specific research question.
Use contrasting sources to demonstrate that authority is contextual rather than universal.
Teach lateral reading by investigating an unfamiliar source through independent information before accepting its self-description.
Model tracing statistics, quotations, and images to their original publications or contexts.
Explicitly distinguish independent corroboration from multiple outlets repeating a shared source.
Teach students to evaluate the population, sample, methods, date, and limitations of research-based claims.
Introduce correlation and causation through accessible examples that reveal how headlines may overstate research findings.
Use historical and contemporary examples to demonstrate how misconceptions can persist through repeated reporting.
Teach students to compare conflicting evidence without assuming that disagreement automatically means one source is dishonest.
Model identifying bias through framing, word choice, evidence selection, omissions, institutional affiliations, and funding.
Avoid reducing source evaluation to a mechanical checklist or a simple reliable-versus-unreliable classification.
Require students to explain how specific evidence supports their judgments about sources.
Use synthesis matrices to help students organize evidence around ideas rather than around the order in which sources were discovered.
Teach students to select evidence according to its relevance and explanatory power rather than its length or emotional impact.
Model how a researcher revises a claim after encountering persuasive contradictory evidence.
Teach students to distinguish primary textual evidence from secondary contextual or critical interpretations in literary analysis.
Model direct quotation, paraphrase, and summary as different choices serving different writing purposes.
Use side-by-side examples to distinguish effective paraphrasing from patchwriting.

vocabulary.definition: A text that presents connected events or experiences through storytelling.
vocabulary.example: A memoir recounts a formative childhood experience and reflects on its lasting significance.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate storytelling choice used to develop meaning, shape reader experience, or achieve a purpose.
vocabulary.example: An author delays revealing a character's identity to create suspense and encourage readers to reconsider earlier events.

vocabulary.definition: The organized sequence of events and relationships among events in a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A character's decision to conceal a mistake creates consequences that drive the remaining events.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement and organization of narrative events.
vocabulary.example: A story begins with its ending and gradually reveals the events that produced that outcome.

vocabulary.definition: An organization in which events are presented primarily in the order in which they occur.
vocabulary.example: A coming-of-age story follows a character from the beginning of a school year through graduation.

vocabulary.definition: An organization in which events are presented outside their chronological sequence.
vocabulary.example: A narrative alternates between a character's childhood and adult life to reveal connections between past and present.

vocabulary.definition: A narrative structure in which an outer story contains one or more additional stories.
vocabulary.example: A traveler recounts an earlier adventure to a group of listeners, creating a story within a story.

vocabulary.definition: A narrative organization in which the ending returns to an image, situation, setting, or idea introduced at the beginning.
vocabulary.example: A story begins and ends at the same train station, but the protagonist understands the place differently after the intervening events.

vocabulary.definition: Two or more related storylines that develop alongside one another.
vocabulary.example: A novel follows two siblings whose separate experiences reveal contrasting responses to a shared family conflict.

vocabulary.definition: Narrative information that establishes relevant characters, setting, circumstances, or background.
vocabulary.example: The opening scene introduces a family preparing to leave its longtime home.

vocabulary.definition: An event that disrupts the initial situation and initiates a central conflict.
vocabulary.example: A mysterious letter forces a character to investigate a family secret.

vocabulary.definition: Developments that intensify conflict, complicate circumstances, or increase narrative tension.
vocabulary.example: Each attempt to conceal a mistake creates a more serious problem for the protagonist.

vocabulary.definition: A decisive moment or turning point in the development of a narrative's central conflict.
vocabulary.example: A character must choose between protecting a friendship and revealing an important truth.

vocabulary.definition: The portion of a narrative that establishes the consequences or outcome of its central conflict.
vocabulary.example: After admitting a mistake, a character begins rebuilding a damaged relationship.

vocabulary.definition: A narrative shift to an event that occurred before the current point in the story.
vocabulary.example: A character's encounter with an abandoned house triggers a memory that explains a present fear.

vocabulary.definition: A narrative shift that presents events occurring later than the current point in the story.
vocabulary.example: A brief scene from the protagonist's future reveals consequences that the remaining narrative will explain.

vocabulary.definition: The introduction of details that suggest or prepare readers for later developments.
vocabulary.example: Repeated references to a weakening bridge prepare readers for a later accident.

vocabulary.definition: The position or viewpoint through which a story is presented and understood.
vocabulary.example: Two characters describe the same argument differently because each interprets the other's actions through personal assumptions.

vocabulary.definition: Narration presented by a speaker who uses first-person pronouns and participates in or observes the events.
vocabulary.example: A narrator describes a family disagreement using I and explains personal reactions to the conflict.

vocabulary.definition: Narration that addresses the central participant or reader as you.
vocabulary.example: A story invites the reader to experience a character's decisions through direct second-person address.

vocabulary.definition: Third-person narration primarily restricted to the knowledge, perceptions, or thoughts of a particular character.
vocabulary.example: Readers understand one character's fears but must infer what other characters are thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Third-person narration that can present knowledge of multiple characters' thoughts, experiences, or circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A narrator reveals the conflicting private motivations of two characters involved in the same dispute.

vocabulary.definition: The presentation of events, ideas, or experiences through more than one viewpoint.
vocabulary.example: Alternating chapters reveal how two friends interpret the same misunderstanding.

vocabulary.definition: A narrator whose account is limited, distorted, misleading, or otherwise not fully trustworthy.
vocabulary.example: A narrator insists that every decision was reasonable, although the described events reveal increasingly irrational behavior.

vocabulary.definition: The degree of emotional, psychological, or observational closeness between the narrative voice and a character or event.
vocabulary.example: A distant description summarizes a character's grief, while a closer perspective reveals immediate thoughts and sensations.

vocabulary.definition: A recurring character, image, situation, or narrative pattern recognizable across literary works and traditions.
vocabulary.example: A mentor guides an inexperienced protagonist through a difficult transformation.

vocabulary.definition: A recognizable category of character associated with recurring traits, roles, or functions.
vocabulary.example: The outsider challenges the expectations of an established community.

vocabulary.definition: A central character whose experiences, goals, or conflicts organize a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A young musician struggles to balance family expectations with personal ambitions.

vocabulary.definition: A character, group, institution, force, or condition that opposes a protagonist's goals.
vocabulary.example: A restrictive social system prevents a character from pursuing an education.

vocabulary.definition: A character whose contrasting qualities help reveal or emphasize another character's traits.
vocabulary.example: A cautious friend highlights the protagonist's impulsiveness.

vocabulary.definition: A character who undergoes meaningful internal change during a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A character who initially values approval learns to act according to personal convictions.

vocabulary.definition: A character whose central beliefs, personality, or motivations remain relatively stable throughout a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A principled mentor maintains the same ethical commitments despite changing circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: A multidimensional character developed through varied traits, motivations, experiences, or contradictions.
vocabulary.example: A generous character also struggles with jealousy and a desire for recognition.

vocabulary.definition: A character developed through a relatively limited set of traits or functions.
vocabulary.example: A minor official appears primarily to enforce a rule that creates an obstacle for the protagonist.

vocabulary.definition: The pattern of a character's development, transformation, or response to experience across a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A protagonist gradually moves from avoiding responsibility to accepting the consequences of personal choices.

vocabulary.definition: The desire, belief, need, fear, or goal that influences a character's actions.
vocabulary.example: A character conceals the truth because of a fear of disappointing a parent.

vocabulary.definition: Explicit description of a character's traits or qualities.
vocabulary.example: The narrator directly describes a character as impatient and ambitious.

vocabulary.definition: The development of character through actions, dialogue, thoughts, relationships, appearance, or others' responses.
vocabulary.example: A character repeatedly interrupts conversations, revealing impatience without the narrator naming the trait.

vocabulary.definition: A struggle involving competing desires, beliefs, emotions, or decisions within a character.
vocabulary.example: A student struggles between loyalty to a friend and a commitment to honesty.

vocabulary.definition: A struggle between a character and an outside person, group, institution, environment, or force.
vocabulary.example: A family faces eviction because of economic conditions beyond its immediate control.

vocabulary.definition: The time, place, physical environment, and social or cultural circumstances of a narrative.
vocabulary.example: A story set in a small town during a period of economic decline presents different opportunities and pressures than a story set in a prosperous city.

vocabulary.definition: The emotional atmosphere or feeling created for readers through narrative details and language.
vocabulary.example: Empty streets, flickering lights, and distant footsteps create an unsettling mood.

vocabulary.definition: The attitude conveyed by a narrator, speaker, or text toward its subject or audience.
vocabulary.example: A narrator describes an extravagant celebration with skeptical and ironic language.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes sensory experience.
vocabulary.example: Descriptions of damp stone, cold air, and the smell of smoke establish the atmosphere of an abandoned building.

vocabulary.definition: The use of an object, image, action, character, or setting to suggest meaning beyond its literal function.
vocabulary.example: A locked gate gradually comes to represent the restrictions placed on a character's independence.

vocabulary.definition: A recurring image, idea, phrase, situation, or other element that contributes to a text's meaning.
vocabulary.example: Repeated references to unfinished letters reinforce a theme about communication and regret.

vocabulary.definition: A figurative comparison that describes one thing in terms of another without using an explicit comparison word such as like or as.
vocabulary.example: A character describes a family secret as a wall separating the people in the household.

vocabulary.definition: A metaphor developed through multiple related details across a passage or text.
vocabulary.example: A narrative repeatedly presents a damaged garden as a way of exploring the deterioration and restoration of a relationship.

vocabulary.definition: Spoken exchanges between characters.
vocabulary.example: A tense conversation reveals a disagreement that neither character directly acknowledges.

vocabulary.definition: An implied meaning beneath a character's words, actions, or interactions.
vocabulary.example: A character says that a friend's departure is fine while avoiding eye contact and abruptly changing the subject.

vocabulary.definition: A presentation of a character's private thoughts or internal speech.
vocabulary.example: Readers encounter a character's conflicting thoughts immediately before a difficult decision.

vocabulary.definition: The perceived speed at which narrative events, information, and developments unfold.
vocabulary.example: Short sentences and rapid dialogue accelerate a confrontation, while detailed reflection slows the aftermath.

vocabulary.definition: A developed narrative unit that presents a particular event or interaction with relatively immediate detail.
vocabulary.example: A writer presents a difficult conversation through dialogue, gestures, and sensory description.

vocabulary.definition: A compressed account of events that moves through time without developing every moment as a complete scene.
vocabulary.example: Several months of routine practice are summarized before the narrative focuses on a decisive performance.

vocabulary.definition: A situation in which readers or viewers possess significant information that one or more characters do not.
vocabulary.example: Readers know that a trusted character has concealed a betrayal while the protagonist continues to rely on that character.

vocabulary.definition: A meaningful contrast between an expected outcome and what actually occurs.
vocabulary.example: A character's attempt to avoid embarrassment creates the public attention the character feared.

vocabulary.definition: A developed insight or understanding about a significant subject, human experience, or social concern.
vocabulary.example: A narrative suggests that fear of rejection can prevent people from forming honest relationships.

vocabulary.definition: The process through which narrative details, conflicts, character choices, and patterns establish, complicate, or deepen a theme.
vocabulary.example: A theme about belonging develops through an outsider's initial isolation, changing relationships, and final decision to define belonging independently.

vocabulary.definition: The meaningful relationship between a text's ideas and broader societal experiences, concerns, institutions, or values.
vocabulary.example: A story about exclusion can illuminate contemporary questions about community membership and social responsibility.

vocabulary.definition: The relationships among texts through references, adaptations, shared patterns, or other forms of influence.
vocabulary.example: A contemporary novel reworks the events and character roles of an ancient myth.

vocabulary.definition: A new version of an existing story or text that changes its form, setting, perspective, language, or other elements.
vocabulary.example: A modern novel retells a traditional epic from the perspective of a previously marginalized character.

vocabulary.definition: The intended or reasonably inferred function of a writer's choices in relation to meaning, audience, and context.
vocabulary.example: An author uses contrasting perspectives to encourage readers to question simplified judgments about a conflict.

vocabulary.definition: Specific details, quotations, events, or patterns from a text used to support an interpretation or evaluation.
vocabulary.example: A student cites a character's changing responses to a recurring image to explain thematic development.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned evaluation of a literary work's choices, effects, strengths, limitations, or effectiveness.
vocabulary.example: A student evaluates whether a delayed revelation deepens a story's central conflict or merely creates an artificial surprise.

targets: I can identify significant narrative techniques and explain how they work together.
I can evaluate how archetypes, perspectives, plot structure, and symbolism contribute to meaning.
I can explain how changing the narrative perspective changes readers' understanding.
I can evaluate whether an author's structural choices effectively support a narrative's purpose.
I can explain how conflict, dialogue, diction, and imagery contribute to characterization and meaning.
I can distinguish a thematic statement from a topic or plot summary.
I can trace a theme through several passages from a literary work.
I can explain how a theme develops, changes, or becomes more complex.
I can evaluate a theme's relevance to broader social concerns using evidence and reasoning.
I can compare thematic development within and across texts.
I can identify narrative patterns and character types shared by literature from different time periods.
I can explain how a later author transforms or challenges an earlier literary pattern.
I can create complex characters whose changes emerge from meaningful experiences and decisions.
I can use setting and sensory details to create a purposeful mood.
I can use metaphors or recurring images to develop a theme across my narrative.
I can select narrative techniques that engage a particular audience and achieve a specific purpose.
I can revise my narrative to strengthen its structure, characterization, mood, and thematic development.
I can justify my literary interpretations and craft decisions with specific evidence and reasoning.

suggestedTexts.title: The Lottery
suggestedTexts.author: Shirley Jackson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate the interaction of ordinary setting, restrained narration, symbolism, foreshadowing, and delayed revelation.
suggestedTexts.access: The New Yorker archive or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible prose; violent subject matter and thematic complexity require preparation.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Why does an apparently ordinary community gather for a tradition that no one seems willing to question?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the familiar setting and understated narrative voice interact with the black box, gathering ritual, and delayed revelation. How do these choices develop a theme about conformity and collective responsibility?

suggestedTexts.title: The Most Dangerous Game
suggestedTexts.author: Richard Connell
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze conflict, pacing, foreshadowing, setting, irony, and the transformation of a familiar hunter archetype.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain literary collections or school anthology
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; support older vocabulary and historical references.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: What happens when a celebrated hunter becomes the prey?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the island setting, initial conversation about hunting, and reversal of character roles work together to develop suspense and complicate the story's treatment of power.

suggestedTexts.title: The Story of an Hour
suggestedTexts.author: Kate Chopin
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze symbolism, restricted perspective, irony, setting, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; historical gender expectations support interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Trace the changing significance of the open window and evaluate how the narrative's restricted perspective and final reversal develop a theme about freedom and social expectations.

suggestedTexts.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
suggestedTexts.author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate unreliable narration, symbolism, setting, interior conflict, and social relevance.
suggestedTexts.access: Project Gutenberg or public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; provide historical medical context and sensitivity around mental health.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: How does a room intended to help a woman recover become central to her deteriorating condition?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the narrator's restricted circumstances, journal-like perspective, and evolving descriptions of the wallpaper interact. Explain how these techniques develop a theme about authority and autonomy.

suggestedTexts.title: The Tell-Tale Heart
suggestedTexts.author: Edgar Allan Poe
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze unreliable narration, repetition, pacing, diction, symbolism, and psychological conflict.
suggestedTexts.access: Project Gutenberg or public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; includes murder and psychological distress.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the narrator's insistence on rationality interacts with fragmented syntax, repeated details, and escalating sensory descriptions. What does the narration reveal beyond the narrator's intended explanation?

suggestedTexts.title: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge
suggestedTexts.author: Ambrose Bierce
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate nonlinear structure, narrative perspective, manipulation of time, and delayed revelation.
suggestedTexts.access: Project Gutenberg or public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to challenging; includes execution and war.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Reconstruct the chronological sequence of events. Evaluate how the author's manipulation of narrative time and perspective shapes readers' emotional investment and understanding of the ending.

suggestedTexts.title: The Necklace
suggestedTexts.author: Guy de Maupassant
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze character motivation, symbolism, social conflict, situational irony, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain translations or school anthology
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; translation affects reading difficulty.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the necklace, social setting, protagonist's desires, and final revelation interact to develop a theme about status, appearance, and consequence.

suggestedTexts.title: The Gift of the Magi
suggestedTexts.author: O. Henry
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze parallel character motivations, symbolism, irony, and narrative purpose.
suggestedTexts.access: Project Gutenberg or public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; explain historical vocabulary and the biblical allusion.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Compare the symbolic significance of the watch and hair. Evaluate how the parallel decisions and ironic ending develop a theme about generosity and value.

suggestedTexts.title: The Open Boat
suggestedTexts.author: Stephen Crane
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate environmental conflict, group characterization, setting, imagery, and philosophical theme.
suggestedTexts.access: Project Gutenberg or public-domain literary collections
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Challenging; support sentence structure and naturalist literary context.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Analyze how the sea functions as both a physical setting and a force shaping the characters' understanding of their circumstances. Evaluate the relationship between environmental conflict and the story's treatment of human solidarity.

suggestedTexts.title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
suggestedTexts.author: Ursula K. Le Guin

suggestedTexts.access: Licensed anthology or school library
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to challenging; includes disturbing treatment of a child.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Would you accept a perfect society if its happiness depended on one person's suffering?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the narrator's invitation to imagine the city interacts with the later revelation of suffering. How does the structure challenge readers' assumptions about collective happiness and moral responsibility?

suggestedTexts.title: The Paper Menagerie
suggestedTexts.author: Ken Liu
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze magical realism, retrospective narration, symbolism, cultural identity, and character change.

suggestedTexts.interestHook: What can a childhood collection of magical paper animals reveal about family, language, and belonging?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Trace the changing significance of the paper animals across the story. Evaluate how retrospective narration, magical elements, and the final revelation develop themes about cultural identity and regret.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the familiar technological setting and escalating conflict develop a theme about convenience, privacy, and personal choice.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the automated house, recurring imagery of the veldt, and escalating family conflict develop a warning about dependence on technology.

suggestedTexts.title: There Will Come Soft Rains
