vocabulary.definition: Literary expression that uses concentrated language, sound, structure, imagery, and other techniques to communicate meaning or create an experience.
vocabulary.example: A poem uses recurring images of changing seasons to explore memory and loss.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate choice involving language, sound, structure, imagery, or presentation that contributes to a poem's effects.
vocabulary.example: A poet places a significant word at the end of a line to emphasize its importance.

vocabulary.definition: An established practice or recognizable feature associated with poetry or a particular poetic form.
vocabulary.example: A traditional English sonnet commonly contains fourteen lines and a concluding couplet.

vocabulary.definition: The organizational pattern or structural design of a poem.
vocabulary.example: A villanelle uses a recurring pattern of refrains and rhyme.

vocabulary.definition: Poetry that primarily expresses a speaker's thoughts, feelings, perceptions, or reflections.
vocabulary.example: A speaker reflects on the emotional significance of returning to a childhood home.

vocabulary.definition: Poetry that presents a sequence of connected events or tells a story.
vocabulary.example: A ballad recounts a journey that ends in an unexpected loss.

vocabulary.definition: A poem in which a fictional or constructed speaker addresses an implied or identifiable listener, often revealing aspects of the speaker's character.
vocabulary.example: A powerful speaker describes a past relationship while unintentionally revealing controlling behavior.

vocabulary.definition: A fourteen-line poetic form with conventions that vary among traditions, often involving a developed idea and a significant turn.
vocabulary.example: An English sonnet develops a comparison across three quatrains and concludes with a couplet.

vocabulary.definition: A sonnet commonly organized into an octave and a sestet, often with a shift in thought between them.
vocabulary.example: The octave presents a problem, and the sestet develops a response or reconsideration.

vocabulary.definition: An English sonnet commonly organized into three quatrains and a concluding couplet, traditionally using the rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.
vocabulary.example: Three quatrains develop different aspects of an argument, and the final couplet offers a concluding insight.

vocabulary.definition: A narrative poem or song, often characterized by recurring stanzas, strong rhythm, repetition, and a memorable story.
vocabulary.example: A poem recounts a dramatic event through alternating dialogue and narrative description.

vocabulary.definition: A poem that addresses, celebrates, examines, or reflects upon a subject with sustained attention.
vocabulary.example: A poet addresses an ordinary household object and explores its unexpected significance.

vocabulary.definition: A poem reflecting on loss, death, remembrance, or mourning.
vocabulary.example: A speaker remembers a deceased friend through images of familiar shared places.

vocabulary.definition: A short poetic form originating in Japan, traditionally associated with a concentrated image, seasonal awareness, and a meaningful juxtaposition; English-language adaptations vary.
vocabulary.example: A brief poem juxtaposes an autumn leaf with the movement of a passing train.

vocabulary.definition: A nineteen-line poetic form consisting of five tercets and a concluding quatrain, with two recurring refrains and a prescribed rhyme pattern.
vocabulary.example: Two repeated lines acquire increasingly complex meanings as the poem develops.

vocabulary.definition: Poetry that does not follow a fixed metrical or rhyme scheme but uses purposeful rhythm, lineation, and other structural choices.
vocabulary.example: A poem uses varying line lengths and repeated images to create movement and emphasis.

vocabulary.definition: Unrhymed poetry written in a regular meter, most commonly iambic pentameter in English literature.
vocabulary.example: A dramatic speech uses five iambic feet per line without a regular end-rhyme pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A poetic composition presented in prose paragraphs while using concentrated imagery, figurative language, rhythm, or other poetic techniques.
vocabulary.example: A short paragraph develops an extended metaphor through rhythmic sentences and compressed imagery.

vocabulary.definition: Poetry composed or presented with particular attention to oral performance, voice, rhythm, and audience engagement.
vocabulary.example: A performer uses changes in pace, volume, repetition, and gesture to emphasize a poem's central idea.

vocabulary.definition: A unit of poetic language whose ending may be determined by meaning, rhythm, visual design, or other artistic choices.
vocabulary.example: A poet isolates a single word on a line to create emphasis.

vocabulary.definition: A grouping of poetic lines that functions as a structural unit.
vocabulary.example: A poem uses separate stanzas to distinguish childhood memories from adult reflections.

vocabulary.definition: Two consecutive poetic lines functioning as a unit.
vocabulary.example: A sonnet ends with a couplet that offers a final reconsideration of the preceding ideas.

vocabulary.definition: A stanza or grouping of three poetic lines.
vocabulary.example: A poem develops its central image through a sequence of tercets.

vocabulary.definition: A stanza or grouping of four poetic lines.
vocabulary.example: Each quatrain develops a different aspect of a speaker's argument.

vocabulary.definition: A grouping of six poetic lines, often associated with the concluding portion of a Petrarchan sonnet.
vocabulary.example: A sestet responds to the emotional problem established in an octave.

vocabulary.definition: A grouping of eight poetic lines, often associated with the opening portion of a Petrarchan sonnet.
vocabulary.example: An octave develops a description that the remaining six lines reinterpret.

vocabulary.definition: A line, phrase, or group of lines repeated at intervals throughout a poem.
vocabulary.example: A repeated question becomes more urgent each time it appears.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement and division of language into poetic lines.
vocabulary.example: A poet breaks a sentence immediately before an unexpected word to delay its revelation.

vocabulary.definition: The continuation of a grammatical unit or thought beyond the end of a poetic line without a strong concluding pause.
vocabulary.example: The first line ends with a verb, and its object appears at the beginning of the next line.

vocabulary.definition: A poetic line that concludes with a significant grammatical or rhetorical pause.
vocabulary.example: A line ends with a complete sentence and a period.

vocabulary.definition: A significant pause or break within a poetic line.
vocabulary.example: A dash interrupts a line to create hesitation before a speaker's admission.

vocabulary.definition: The unprinted space surrounding or separating elements of a poem, which may contribute to pacing, emphasis, visual design, or meaning.
vocabulary.example: A large gap separates two contrasting images and encourages a longer pause.

vocabulary.definition: The perceived pattern of movement, stress, duration, and pause in language.
vocabulary.example: Repeated short phrases create a quick, insistent rhythm.

vocabulary.definition: A recurring organizational pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables or other rhythmic units in poetry.
vocabulary.example: A poem establishes a regular pattern of five iambs per line.

vocabulary.definition: A recurring unit of stressed and unstressed syllables used to describe meter in English poetry.
vocabulary.example: An iamb consists of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.

vocabulary.definition: A metrical foot consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
vocabulary.example: The word begin commonly illustrates an iambic stress pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A metrical foot consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable.
vocabulary.example: The word garden commonly illustrates a trochaic stress pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A metrical foot consisting of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable.
vocabulary.example: The word understand can illustrate an anapestic stress pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A metrical foot consisting of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables.
vocabulary.example: The word beautiful commonly illustrates a dactylic stress pattern.

vocabulary.definition: A metrical pattern consisting primarily of five iambic feet per line.
vocabulary.example: Many Shakespearean sonnets establish iambic pentameter while allowing meaningful rhythmic variation.

vocabulary.definition: The process of examining and marking the rhythmic or metrical patterns of poetic language.
vocabulary.example: A student marks stressed and unstressed syllables to examine a line's relationship to an established meter.

vocabulary.definition: A correspondence between sounds in words, especially stressed vowel sounds and the sounds that follow them.
vocabulary.example: Light and night form a perfect rhyme.

vocabulary.definition: The pattern of end rhymes in a poem, commonly represented with letters.
vocabulary.example: A four-line stanza with alternating rhymes follows an ABAB pattern.

vocabulary.definition: Rhyme occurring at the ends of poetic lines.
vocabulary.example: Two lines conclude with the words rain and train.

vocabulary.definition: Rhyme occurring within a line or between an internal word and another word in a poem.
vocabulary.example: The phrase bright light appears within a single line.

vocabulary.definition: An approximate rhyme involving related but not fully matching sounds.
vocabulary.example: The words shape and keep share a final consonant sound but differ in their vowel sounds.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words.
vocabulary.example: Silver streams slip silently.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words.
vocabulary.example: The low road home repeats a long o sound.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of consonant sounds within or at the ends of nearby words.
vocabulary.example: The words blank, think, and trunk repeat a final consonant cluster.

vocabulary.definition: The use of words whose sounds imitate or suggest the sounds they describe.
vocabulary.example: The words hiss, buzz, and clang evoke recognizable sounds.

vocabulary.definition: The deliberate recurrence of words, phrases, sounds, images, or structures.
vocabulary.example: A poet repeats a phrase at the beginning of successive lines to emphasize a developing idea.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines, clauses, or sentences.
vocabulary.example: Several lines begin with the phrase I remember.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of a word or phrase at the ends of successive lines, clauses, or sentences.
vocabulary.example: Several lines conclude with the phrase not yet.

vocabulary.definition: A combination of sounds perceived as smooth, harmonious, or pleasing in a particular context.
vocabulary.example: Flowing vowel sounds and soft consonants contribute to a peaceful description.

vocabulary.definition: A combination of sounds perceived as harsh, discordant, or jarring in a particular context.
vocabulary.example: Abrupt consonant clusters and sharp sound patterns contribute to a description of mechanical destruction.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes sensory experience or creates a vivid mental impression.
vocabulary.example: The smell of wet pavement and the warmth of afternoon sunlight establish a recognizable setting.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes the sense of sight.
vocabulary.example: A narrow stripe of gold light crosses a darkened room.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes the sense of hearing.
vocabulary.example: A distant bell echoes through an empty station.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes the sense of touch or physical sensation.
vocabulary.example: Rough wool scratches against a speaker's wrist.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes the sense of smell.
vocabulary.example: The scent of orange blossoms drifts through an open window.

vocabulary.definition: Language that evokes the sense of taste.
vocabulary.example: A bitter trace of coffee remains on the speaker's tongue.

vocabulary.definition: Language that communicates meaning through comparisons, associations, or expressions beyond straightforward literal description.
vocabulary.example: A speaker describes regret as a shadow that follows every decision.

vocabulary.definition: A figurative comparison that explicitly uses a comparison word such as like or as.
vocabulary.example: The abandoned house stood like a forgotten photograph.

vocabulary.definition: A figurative comparison that presents one thing in terms of another without an explicit comparison word such as like or as.
vocabulary.example: The city is a restless machine.

vocabulary.definition: A metaphor developed through multiple related details across a passage or complete text.
vocabulary.example: A poem compares memory to an old house, developing the comparison through rooms, windows, keys, and locked doors.

vocabulary.definition: The attribution of human qualities or actions to nonhuman things, forces, or abstract ideas.
vocabulary.example: The wind argues with the windows.

vocabulary.definition: Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or expressive effect.
vocabulary.example: The speaker claims to have waited a thousand years for a reply.

vocabulary.definition: The deliberate presentation of something as less significant or intense than it actually is.
vocabulary.example: A speaker describes a devastating disappointment as a small inconvenience.

vocabulary.definition: An apparently contradictory statement or situation that may reveal a meaningful insight.
vocabulary.example: A speaker discovers that letting go of a possession makes its significance more enduring.

vocabulary.definition: A compact combination of apparently contradictory terms.
vocabulary.example: The phrase deafening silence combines contrasting ideas.

vocabulary.definition: The use of an image, object, action, or other element to suggest meanings beyond its literal function.
vocabulary.example: An unopened letter may represent an unresolved relationship when supported by the poem's context.

vocabulary.definition: A recurring image, idea, phrase, or pattern that contributes to a text's meaning.
vocabulary.example: Repeated references to doors reinforce a poem's exploration of opportunity and exclusion.

vocabulary.definition: A reference to another text, historical event, cultural figure, myth, or other recognizable source.
vocabulary.example: A poem refers to Icarus to develop an idea about ambition and its consequences.

vocabulary.definition: A direct address to an absent person, abstract idea, object, or nonhuman entity.
vocabulary.example: A speaker directly addresses time as though it could respond.

vocabulary.definition: A meaningful contrast between appearance and reality, expectation and outcome, or literal expression and intended meaning.
vocabulary.example: A speaker praises a supposedly perfect city while describing evidence of widespread suffering.

vocabulary.definition: The placement of contrasting or related elements near one another to create a meaningful relationship.
vocabulary.example: A poem places an image of a lavish banquet beside an image of an empty kitchen.

vocabulary.definition: A writer's selection and use of words.
vocabulary.example: A poet selects words associated with decay to establish an atmosphere of deterioration.

vocabulary.definition: The literal or primary meaning of a word.
vocabulary.example: A house is a building used as a place of residence.

vocabulary.definition: The emotional, cultural, or associative meanings connected with a word beyond its literal definition.
vocabulary.example: The word home may suggest belonging, safety, or memory.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of words and grammatical structures within phrases, clauses, and sentences.
vocabulary.example: A poet delays the main verb to create suspense before completing a thought.

vocabulary.definition: The voice or constructed perspective through which a poem is expressed.
vocabulary.example: A poem may be spoken by a fictional character whose beliefs differ from those of the poet.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberately constructed identity or character adopted by a poetic speaker.
vocabulary.example: A poet writes from the perspective of an aging tree observing changes in a city.

vocabulary.definition: The distinctive qualities of expression created through a poem's diction, syntax, perspective, rhythm, and attitude.
vocabulary.example: A conversational voice uses direct address, informal language, and irregular line lengths.

vocabulary.definition: The attitude conveyed by a speaker or text toward its subject, audience, or situation.
vocabulary.example: A speaker describes a childhood memory with affectionate but regretful language.

vocabulary.definition: The emotional atmosphere or experience created for readers or listeners.
vocabulary.example: Dark imagery and abrupt pauses create an atmosphere of uncertainty.

vocabulary.definition: A developed insight or understanding about a significant subject, experience, or concern.
vocabulary.example: A poem suggests that remembering the past can preserve connections while also intensifying loss.

vocabulary.definition: A significant turn or shift in thought, perspective, argument, or emotional direction within a poem.
vocabulary.example: A sonnet moves from describing an apparent problem to reconsidering its meaning.

vocabulary.definition: The presence of more than one plausible meaning or interpretation.
vocabulary.example: A reference to a closing door may suggest either protection or exclusion.

vocabulary.definition: The concentration of meaning into relatively few words through precise language, implication, imagery, and structure.
vocabulary.example: A brief image of an untouched place setting communicates absence without explicitly explaining a loss.

vocabulary.definition: An evidence-based evaluation of how a poem's artistic choices contribute to its meaning, purpose, or effectiveness.
vocabulary.example: A student evaluates how a repeated refrain becomes increasingly ironic as a poem develops.

vocabulary.definition: The oral or embodied presentation of a poem through choices involving voice, timing, emphasis, gesture, and delivery.
vocabulary.example: A reader slows before a poem's final line to emphasize a shift in meaning.

targets: I can identify a poem's speaker, situation, subject, and significant structural features.
I can distinguish a poem's speaker from its poet.
I can explain how a poem's form contributes to its meaning.
I can analyze how line breaks and stanza organization influence emphasis and interpretation.
I can evaluate the effects of enjambment, caesura, and end-stopped lines.
I can analyze patterns of rhyme, rhythm, meter, and sound.
I can explain how changes in sound or rhythm influence meaning.
I can interpret imagery, symbolism, and figurative language using evidence.
I can trace how an extended metaphor develops across a poem.
I can explain how diction and connotation contribute to poetic voice and tone.
I can identify a significant shift in a poem and evaluate its effect.
I can develop and support a defensible thematic interpretation.
I can evaluate how multiple poetic techniques work together to develop meaning.
I can compare how different poems address related ideas through different artistic choices.
I can discuss alternative interpretations respectfully and evaluate their textual support.
I can critique a poem using explicit criteria and relevant evidence.
I can evaluate how oral performance influences interpretation.
I can select poetic techniques appropriate to a specific audience and purpose.
I can create a poem using purposeful imagery, figurative language, sound, and structure.
I can follow or adapt poetic conventions to achieve an intended effect.
I can revise my poem to strengthen its language, organization, sound, and meaning.
I can explain how my poetic choices contribute to the experience I want to create.

suggestedTexts.title: Sonnet 18
suggestedTexts.author: William Shakespeare
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate sonnet structure, extended comparison, imagery, meter, rhyme, and the concluding couplet.
suggestedTexts.access: Folger Shakespeare Library or public-domain editions
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; support Early Modern English vocabulary.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the poem develops and complicates its initial comparison. Explain how the concluding couplet transforms the poem's treatment of beauty, time, and artistic preservation.

suggestedTexts.title: Sonnet 130
suggestedTexts.author: William Shakespeare
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze irony, unconventional imagery, comparison, poetic conventions, and the concluding turn.
suggestedTexts.access: Folger Shakespeare Library or public-domain editions
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; explain conventional Renaissance love poetry.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Can a love poem be more convincing when it refuses to idealize its subject?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how Shakespeare challenges conventional romantic comparisons while retaining the sonnet form. Explain how the final couplet reshapes the reader's understanding of the preceding descriptions.

suggestedTexts.title: Ozymandias
suggestedTexts.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze framed narration, irony, imagery, symbolism, sonnet structure, and themes of power and impermanence.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; support vocabulary and historical context.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the ruined statue, its inscription, the surrounding landscape, and the poem's layered voices interact to challenge claims of permanent political power.

suggestedTexts.title: The World Is Too Much with Us
suggestedTexts.author: William Wordsworth
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze octave-sestet structure, allusion, personification, tone, and social criticism.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to challenging; explain mythological references.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the sonnet's structural turn and mythological allusions develop its criticism of materialism and humanity's relationship with nature.

suggestedTexts.title: Hope is the thing with feathers
suggestedTexts.author: Emily Dickinson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, compressed imagery, sound, punctuation, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation; consult a reliable edition for punctuation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Trace the bird metaphor across the poem. Evaluate how the image develops from a description of hope into an exploration of endurance and generosity.

suggestedTexts.title: Because I could not stop for Death
suggestedTexts.author: Emily Dickinson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze personification, symbolism, narrative progression, meter, slant rhyme, and ambiguity.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; support unfamiliar syntax and abstract interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the personification of Death and the journey's changing images complicate conventional expectations about mortality. Consider how rhythm and punctuation influence the poem's atmosphere.

suggestedTexts.title: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
suggestedTexts.author: Emily Dickinson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze direct address, irony, diction, sound, and social commentary.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.interestHook: What if being unknown is more desirable than being famous?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how conversational diction, direct address, and the comparison involving a frog develop the speaker's attitude toward public recognition.

suggestedTexts.title: The Raven
suggestedTexts.author: Edgar Allan Poe
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze refrain, internal rhyme, meter, alliteration, symbolism, atmosphere, and escalating psychological conflict.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to challenging; support vocabulary and oral reading.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: How can one repeated word become increasingly disturbing?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the recurring refrain acquires new significance as the speaker's questions change. Explain how sound patterns, imagery, and structure intensify the poem's exploration of grief.

suggestedTexts.title: Annabel Lee
suggestedTexts.author: Edgar Allan Poe
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze repetition, rhythm, rhyme, idealized imagery, speaker perspective, and themes of love and loss.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how repeated phrases and musical sound patterns contribute to the speaker's presentation of love and grief. Consider whether the poem's speaker invites sympathy, questioning, or both.

suggestedTexts.title: The Road Not Taken
suggestedTexts.author: Robert Frost
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, ambiguity, irony, retrospective narration, and thematic interpretation.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible language with substantial interpretive complexity.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Compare the descriptions of the two roads with the speaker's imagined future account. Evaluate how the poem complicates familiar interpretations about individuality and decision-making.

suggestedTexts.title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
suggestedTexts.author: Robert Frost
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze interlocking rhyme, meter, imagery, repetition, and tension between desire and obligation.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the poem's regular sound patterns and final repetition contribute to the tension between the speaker's attraction to the woods and continuing obligations.

suggestedTexts.title: Mending Wall
suggestedTexts.author: Robert Frost
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze conversational voice, blank verse, symbolism, contrasting perspectives, and recurring statements.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the physical wall becomes a means of exploring boundaries, tradition, and relationships. Explain how the speaker's questions interact with the neighbor's repeated assertion.

suggestedTexts.title: We Wear the Mask
suggestedTexts.author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, refrain, collective voice, irony, and historical context.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; provide context concerning racial oppression in the United States.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the mask metaphor, collective pronouns, and repeated refrain develop a theme about the difference between public appearance and private experience.

suggestedTexts.title: Sympathy
suggestedTexts.author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, sensory imagery, repetition, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Trace the development of the caged bird image across the poem. Evaluate how repetition and contrasting sensory details communicate the speaker's understanding of confinement and longing.

suggestedTexts.title: Harlem
suggestedTexts.author: Langston Hughes
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze simile, imagery, rhetorical questioning, lineation, and thematic escalation.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible language; historical context deepens interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the sequence of sensory comparisons develops the consequences of deferred aspirations. Explain how the final question changes the emotional and thematic direction of the poem.

suggestedTexts.title: Mother to Son
suggestedTexts.author: Langston Hughes
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, poetic voice, vernacular language, direct address, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the staircase metaphor and the mother's distinctive voice communicate the difficulty and necessity of perseverance. Discuss how the poem's conversational form supports its purpose.

suggestedTexts.title: The Negro Speaks of Rivers
suggestedTexts.author: Langston Hughes
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze allusion, repetition, collective identity, imagery, and historical continuity.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible to moderate; provide geographical and historical context.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the recurring river imagery and references to different civilizations expand the poem's speaker beyond an individual identity.

suggestedTexts.title: I, Too
suggestedTexts.author: Langston Hughes
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze allusion, symbolism, structural progression, voice, and assertion of belonging.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible; provide historical context and the relationship to Walt Whitman's poetry.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the kitchen and table imagery, shifts in time, and direct assertion of identity develop the poem's argument about belonging and equality.

suggestedTexts.title: Still I Rise
suggestedTexts.author: Maya Angelou
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze repetition, direct address, simile, rhythm, imagery, and the development of a resilient poetic voice.
suggestedTexts.access: And Still I Rise or authorized publication
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible; historical and cultural context enriches interpretation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how recurring declarations, rhetorical questions, and increasingly expansive imagery develop the speaker's response to oppression and exclusion.

suggestedTexts.title: Caged Bird
suggestedTexts.author: Maya Angelou
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze contrasting imagery, symbolism, repetition, stanza structure, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Shaker, Why Don't You Sing? or authorized publication
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Compare the images associated with the free bird and the caged bird. Evaluate how structural alternation and the recurring song develop the poem's treatment of freedom and constraint.

suggestedTexts.title: The Bean Eaters
suggestedTexts.author: Gwendolyn Brooks
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze compressed imagery, diction, sound, ordinary objects, and implied characterization.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how ordinary household details and the final accumulation of remembered objects develop an understanding of the couple's lives without an extensive narrative explanation.

suggestedTexts.title: We Real Cool
suggestedTexts.author: Gwendolyn Brooks
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze enjambment, repetition, rhythm, rhyme, collective voice, and structural disruption.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or authorized publication
suggestedTexts.interestHook: How can the placement of one repeated word change the meaning of an entire poem?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the placement of the recurring pronoun, the short lines, and the final structural departure shape the reader's understanding of the speakers' identity and vulnerability.

suggestedTexts.title: Those Winter Sundays
suggestedTexts.author: Robert Hayden
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze auditory and tactile imagery, diction, retrospective perspective, and thematic development.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the poem's images of cold, labor, and warmth interact with the speaker's retrospective questions to develop an understanding of unrecognized care.

suggestedTexts.title: The Fish
suggestedTexts.author: Elizabeth Bishop
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended description, imagery, figurative language, tonal shifts, and ethical reflection.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Trace the speaker's changing perception of the fish. Evaluate how detailed imagery and the final shift transform a seemingly ordinary encounter into a reflection on endurance and respect.

suggestedTexts.title: One Art
suggestedTexts.author: Elizabeth Bishop
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze refrain, fixed form, irony, tonal progression, and structural tension.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the recurring claim about loss changes as the examples become increasingly personal. Explain how the fixed form both supports and complicates the speaker's attempt at emotional control.

suggestedTexts.title: Do not go gentle into that good night
suggestedTexts.author: Dylan Thomas
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze refrain, imperative voice, metaphor, contrasting examples, and emotional escalation.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the two refrains interact with the examples of different kinds of men. Explain how the final personal address transforms the poem's broader argument about mortality.

suggestedTexts.title: My Last Duchess
suggestedTexts.author: Robert Browning
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze constructed speaker, dramatic irony, enjambment, rhymed couplets, characterization, and power.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Challenging; support syntax and historical context.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: What can a speaker reveal about himself while trying to impress someone else?
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the Duke's controlled presentation, conversational syntax, and implied revelations expose attitudes that he does not appear to recognize as troubling.

suggestedTexts.title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
suggestedTexts.author: T. S. Eliot
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze allusion, fragmented structure, repetition, imagery, irony, and psychological perspective.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Challenging; use selected passages and contextual support.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how repeated questions, fragmented images, and shifts in perspective develop the speaker's hesitation and anxiety about social judgment.

suggestedTexts.title: The Red Wheelbarrow
suggestedTexts.author: William Carlos Williams
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze lineation, visual imagery, compression, and the significance of ordinary objects.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible vocabulary with substantial interpretive possibilities.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the poem's unusual line breaks, limited diction, and visual arrangement direct attention toward an ordinary scene.

suggestedTexts.title: This Is Just To Say
suggestedTexts.author: William Carlos Williams
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze conversational diction, line breaks, ambiguity, tone, and sensory imagery.
suggestedTexts.access: Poetry Foundation or licensed anthology
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate whether the poem functions as an apology, a celebration of sensory pleasure, or both. Explain how lineation and diction contribute to its ambiguous tone.

suggestedTexts.title: A Noiseless Patient Spider
suggestedTexts.author: Walt Whitman
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze extended metaphor, parallel stanza structure, repetition, and philosophical reflection.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the spider's physical actions develop into a metaphor for the speaker's search for connection. Explain how the two-stanza structure supports the comparison.

suggestedTexts.title: I Hear America Singing
suggestedTexts.author: Walt Whitman
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze cataloging, repetition, parallelism, imagery, and collective identity.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the catalog of workers and recurring references to singing develop a vision of national identity. Compare the poem's inclusions and omissions with Hughes's I, Too.

suggestedTexts.title: The New Colossus
suggestedTexts.author: Emma Lazarus
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze allusion, personification, symbolism, apostrophe, and the structural turn.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; explain the Colossus of Rhodes and historical context.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Evaluate how the poem contrasts traditional monuments of power with a personified figure of welcome. Explain how the structural turn develops the poem's public purpose.

suggestedTexts.title: Dulce et Decorum Est
suggestedTexts.author: Wilfred Owen
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze imagery, sound, irony, allusion, structural shifts, and persuasive purpose.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain editions or Poetry Foundation
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to challenging; includes graphic descriptions of wartime suffering.
