differentiation.title: From Device to Meaning
differentiation.activity: Students identify three poetic techniques in a short accessible poem. They complete an organizer explaining the evidence, immediate effect, and contribution to meaning of each technique. Students revise device-identification statements into analytical statements.
scaffolds: Provide a limited selection of techniques.
Model the difference between identifying a metaphor and explaining its effect.
Use sentence frames connecting evidence to meaning.
differentiation.success: Students explain the effects of at least three poetic techniques using specific textual evidence.

differentiation.title: Hear the Pattern
differentiation.activity: Students listen to and read short poems containing noticeable sound patterns. They mark repeated consonant sounds, vowel sounds, and rhyming words, then explain how one pattern influences the poem's movement or atmosphere.
scaffolds: Model sound identification orally.
Distinguish sounds from letters.
Use color coding to mark different sound patterns.
differentiation.success: Students accurately identify sound patterns and explain a plausible effect within the poem's context.

differentiation.title: Speaker, Subject, and Situation
differentiation.activity: Students read a short poem and identify who is speaking, what situation is presented, what subject is being explored, and what evidence reveals the speaker's attitude. Students distinguish the poem's speaker from its author.
scaffolds: Provide guiding questions about pronouns and direct address.
Model distinguishing the speaker's statements from the poet's biography.
Offer a limited set of tone words with definitions.
differentiation.success: Students develop an evidence-based description of the speaker, situation, and attitude.

differentiation.title: Make the Image Concrete
differentiation.activity: Students revise abstract statements about emotions into short poetic descriptions using sensory details. They compare the effects of direct explanation and concrete imagery.
scaffolds: Model transforming an abstract emotion into a concrete image.
Provide a sensory vocabulary bank.
Allow oral brainstorming before writing.
differentiation.success: Students create precise sensory images that communicate an experience without relying entirely on abstract labels.

differentiation.title: Build an Extended Metaphor
differentiation.activity: Students select a familiar object or activity and connect it to an abstract experience. They develop three related comparisons and organize them into a short poem.
scaffolds: Provide examples of related rather than disconnected comparisons.
Model developing a single comparison through several concrete details.
Use a partially completed planning organizer.
differentiation.success: Students create a coherent extended metaphor that develops meaning across multiple lines.

differentiation.title: The Line Break Laboratory
differentiation.activity: Students examine an existing poem's lineation and compare it with a prose version and an alternative line arrangement. They evaluate how the original line breaks influence emphasis, pacing, ambiguity, and meaning. Students then create two line arrangements for an original short text.
materials: We Real Cool, The Red Wheelbarrow, or another suitable poem
scaffolds: Model how a line ending can temporarily change the reader's interpretation.
Require students to explain specific effects rather than simply identify differences.
Use original teacher-written passages for student rearrangement when permissions are uncertain.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate the effects of lineation and demonstrate purposeful line breaks in their own writing.

differentiation.title: Form and Meaning in the Sonnet
differentiation.activity: Students compare two sonnets, identifying their structural patterns, rhyme schemes, development of ideas, and significant turns. They evaluate how the poets use or adapt formal conventions to achieve different purposes.
materials: Sonnet 18 and Sonnet 130, or another appropriate pairing
scaffolds: Provide vocabulary and historical context.
Model identifying the development of an idea across quatrains.
Distinguish formal description from interpretation of the form's effects.
differentiation.success: Students compare sonnet conventions and evaluate how structural choices contribute to meaning and purpose.

differentiation.title: The Sound of Meaning
differentiation.activity: Students analyze how sound devices interact with imagery and thematic development in a poem. They annotate sound patterns, read selected passages aloud, and write an evaluation explaining the relationship between sound and meaning.
materials: The Raven, Dulce et Decorum Est, or another sound-rich poem
scaffolds: Model analyzing sound within a specific context.
Avoid assigning universal emotional meanings to individual sounds.
Provide a guided oral reading before independent analysis.
differentiation.success: Students explain how sound patterns contribute to a poem's atmosphere, emphasis, or thematic development.

differentiation.title: A Metaphor That Develops
differentiation.activity: Students trace an extended metaphor through several portions of a poem. They identify the central comparison, explain how related details expand its meaning, and evaluate its contribution to the poem's theme.
materials: Mother to Son, Hope is the thing with feathers, or A Noiseless Patient Spider
scaffolds: Model distinguishing the literal image from the abstract idea.
Provide a partially completed metaphor tracker.
Require students to examine how the comparison develops rather than merely identify it.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate how an extended metaphor develops meaning across a complete poem.

differentiation.title: The Turning Point
differentiation.activity: Students identify a significant shift in a poem's tone, imagery, perspective, or argument. They analyze the language and structural choices preceding and following the shift, then evaluate its contribution to the poem's overall meaning.
materials: Ozymandias, The Fish, One Art, or another suitable poem
scaffolds: Model recognizing changes in pronouns, conjunctions, images, and sentence patterns.
Distinguish a formal stanza break from a meaningful shift in thought.
Provide examples of defensible alternative locations for a poem's turn.
differentiation.success: Students support an interpretation of a significant poetic shift and explain its thematic effect.

differentiation.title: Two Poets, One Subject
differentiation.activity: Students compare poems addressing a related subject through different forms, perspectives, or techniques. They develop thematic interpretations and evaluate how each poem's artistic choices contribute to its distinctive meaning.
materials: Sympathy and Caged Bird, or another thematically related pairing
scaffolds: Provide relevant historical and literary context.
Require evidence from both poems.
Model distinguishing a shared subject from identical thematic meaning.
differentiation.success: Students develop a comparative evaluation that explains meaningful similarities and differences in poetic technique and theme.

differentiation.title: Poetry on the Page and in Performance
differentiation.activity: Students read a printed poem and view or listen to an authorized performance. They compare the effects of lineation, punctuation, rhythm, vocal emphasis, tempo, and pauses. Students evaluate how performance choices influence interpretation.
materials: The Hill We Climb or another suitable spoken-word poem
scaffolds: Provide transcripts and captions when available.
Model separating textual techniques from delivery choices.
Require students to identify specific moments supporting their evaluations.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate how textual and performance techniques interact to shape audience experience.

differentiation.title: An Ode to the Ordinary
differentiation.activity: Students select an ordinary object and compose an ode that develops its significance through sensory imagery, figurative language, direct address, and purposeful structure. They explain how their choices transform the object into a meaningful poetic subject.
scaffolds: Begin with detailed observation of the object.
Model moving from literal description to figurative interpretation.
Encourage precise imagery rather than unnecessary elevated vocabulary.
differentiation.success: Students create an original ode in which imagery and figurative language develop a coherent purpose.

differentiation.title: Identity Through Images
differentiation.activity: Students study a poem that develops identity through recurring language and concrete details. They create an original poem using an organizing pattern, sensory images, and purposeful repetition to explore an aspect of identity or belonging.
materials: Where I'm From, Remember, or another appropriate mentor poem
scaffolds: Allow fictional or observational alternatives to personal disclosure.
Provide optional structural patterns without requiring imitation of the mentor poem.
Model connecting concrete details to a larger idea.
differentiation.success: Students create a coherent poem in which specific images and structural choices develop an intended understanding of identity.

differentiation.title: The Refrain That Changes
differentiation.activity: Students analyze how a repeated line develops new significance across a mentor poem. They compose a poem containing a recurring phrase or line whose meaning changes as the surrounding images and ideas develop.
materials: One Art, We Wear the Mask, or another suitable poem
scaffolds: Model distinguishing meaningful repetition from mechanical repetition.
Provide examples of repeated lines that change meaning through context.
Use peer feedback to assess whether the refrain develops across the poem.
differentiation.success: Students use repetition to create structural coherence and meaningful thematic development.

differentiation.title: Poetry Revision Workshop
differentiation.activity: Students draft an original poem for a defined purpose and audience. They revise diction, imagery, figurative language, sound, lineation, and structure. Students submit a revised poem with a craft commentary explaining three significant decisions.
scaffolds: Provide revision examples showing changes beyond spelling and punctuation.
Organize peer feedback around the intended effect of the poem.
Allow students to focus on one major craft element during each revision pass.
differentiation.success: Students produce a purposeful revised poem and explain how their artistic choices contribute to meaning and audience experience.

differentiation.title: Fixed Form as Creative Constraint
differentiation.activity: Students compare poems that use a fixed form to develop different emotional or thematic effects. They evaluate the advantages and limitations of the form, then compose an original poem using or purposefully adapting its conventions.
materials: One Art and Do not go gentle into that good night, or a sonnet pairing
scaffolds: Provide an accurate description of the selected form's conventions.
Require students to distinguish intentional adaptation from accidental inconsistency.
Encourage students to prioritize meaningful language rather than forced rhyme.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate the expressive possibilities of a fixed form and apply its conventions purposefully in an original composition.

differentiation.title: Ambiguity and Competing Interpretations
differentiation.activity: Students develop two plausible interpretations of a poem containing ambiguity, irony, or a complex speaker. They gather evidence for each interpretation, evaluate the strengths and limitations of each reading, and participate in a structured literary discussion.
materials: The Road Not Taken, My Last Duchess, or another complex poem
scaffolds: Distinguish plausible ambiguity from unsupported speculation.
Require evidence that complicates each interpretation.
Model evaluating competing readings without assuming all interpretations are equally supported.
differentiation.success: Students develop and evaluate multiple evidence-based interpretations of a complex poetic text.

differentiation.title: Poetry and the Representation of War
differentiation.activity: Students compare poems that represent war through contrasting imagery, forms, speakers, and purposes. They evaluate how each poem's artistic choices shape its presentation of sacrifice, suffering, remembrance, or national identity.
materials: Credible World War I contextual resources
scaffolds: Provide historical context without substituting it for close reading.
Require students to analyze specific passages from each poem.
Encourage nuanced distinctions among remembrance, patriotism, persuasion, and criticism.
differentiation.success: Students develop a comparative critique explaining how different poetic choices contribute to contrasting representations of war.

differentiation.title: Poetry in Translation
differentiation.activity: Students compare two or more translations of a short poem. They evaluate differences in diction, lineation, imagery, sound, and cultural associations. Students explain how translation choices influence interpretation while recognizing the limitations of evaluating an original language they do not know.
materials: Multiple authorized translations of a selected haiku or lyric poem
scaffolds: Provide the original text when appropriate without requiring students to read an unfamiliar language.
Distinguish translation differences from errors.
Encourage students to evaluate specific effects rather than declare one translation universally superior.
differentiation.success: Students evaluate how translation choices influence poetic form, imagery, and meaning.

differentiation.title: Dramatic Persona Poetry
differentiation.activity: Students compose a dramatic monologue from the perspective of a fictional character whose language reveals more than the character intends. They use diction, syntax, irony, implied audience, and structural choices to develop a complex poetic speaker.
materials: My Last Duchess or another dramatic monologue
scaffolds: Model the distinction between a poet's beliefs and a constructed speaker's perspective.
Require students to plan the speaker's intended message and unintended revelations.
Encourage indirect characterization through language rather than explanatory narration.
differentiation.success: Students create a coherent dramatic monologue in which poetic voice and implied meaning develop a complex speaker.

differentiation.title: Curate a Thematic Poetry Collection
differentiation.activity: Students select four to six poems representing different forms, periods, or cultural traditions that address a related concern. They organize the poems into a purposeful sequence and write an introduction explaining how poetic techniques develop contrasting or complementary thematic perspectives.
scaffolds: Require teacher approval of selections.
Provide guidance on attribution and copyright.
Require specific discussion of poetic techniques rather than thematic summaries alone.
differentiation.success: Students curate a coherent collection and develop an evidence-based explanation of the relationships among form, technique, and theme.

differentiation.title: Write, Perform, and Defend
differentiation.activity: Students create an original spoken-word poem for a defined audience and purpose. They revise the written text, plan vocal delivery, rehearse or record a performance, and submit a commentary explaining how textual and performance choices work together.
scaffolds: Provide alternatives to live public performance.
Model purposeful use of pauses, tempo, emphasis, and intonation.
Evaluate poetic craft separately from performance confidence or presentation style.
differentiation.success: Students produce an original poem and demonstrate purposeful coordination of written techniques and oral delivery.

questions.prompt: A poem describes a person's grief through recurring images of an empty chair, an unopened letter, and a silent telephone. Which interpretation best explains the combined effect of these images?
options: They establish an exact chronological sequence of events.
They use ordinary objects to communicate absence and loss without directly explaining every emotion.
They demonstrate that the poem must follow a fixed rhyme scheme.
They establish that the speaker and poet are necessarily the same person.
questions.answer: They use ordinary objects to communicate absence and loss without directly explaining every emotion.
questions.rationale: The recurring concrete images work together to develop an emotional experience through implication and compression.

questions.prompt: Which statement most clearly evaluates a poetic technique rather than merely identifying it?
options: The poem contains three stanzas.
The poem uses an extended metaphor.
The extended metaphor effectively develops the speaker's growing sense of isolation by transforming familiar household images into signs of absence.
The poet uses several adjectives.
questions.answer: The extended metaphor effectively develops the speaker's growing sense of isolation by transforming familiar household images into signs of absence.
questions.rationale: The response makes a reasoned judgment about how a technique contributes to meaning.

questions.prompt: A poem repeatedly interrupts sentences at unexpected line endings. What should a reader examine to evaluate this technique?
options: Whether every line contains the same number of letters
How the interruptions influence pacing, emphasis, temporary ambiguity, and interpretation
Whether the poet followed every convention of prose paragraphs
How many words appear in the poem's title
questions.answer: How the interruptions influence pacing, emphasis, temporary ambiguity, and interpretation
questions.rationale: Enjambment and lineation influence the way readers encounter and interpret language.

questions.prompt: A poem establishes a regular rhyme scheme but breaks the pattern in its final stanza. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: The poet necessarily made a mistake.
The poem can no longer communicate a theme.
The departure may emphasize a significant change in thought, emotion, or expectation.
The poem automatically becomes a prose poem.
questions.answer: The departure may emphasize a significant change in thought, emotion, or expectation.
questions.rationale: A disruption of an established pattern may be purposeful, although its specific effect must be supported by context.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes rhythm from meter?
options: Rhythm occurs only in rhymed poetry.
Meter is a recurring organizational pattern of rhythmic units, while rhythm refers more broadly to the movement of language.
Rhythm and meter are identical terms for end rhyme.
Free verse contains neither rhythm nor sound patterns.
questions.answer: Meter is a recurring organizational pattern of rhythmic units, while rhythm refers more broadly to the movement of language.
questions.rationale: Poetry may establish meaningful rhythm without following a regular meter.

questions.prompt: A poet uses repeated initial consonant sounds in the phrase silver streams slip silently. Which technique is most directly illustrated?
options: Alliteration
Caesura
Apostrophe
Situational irony
questions.answer: Alliteration
questions.rationale: The phrase repeats an initial consonant sound across nearby words.

questions.prompt: Which analysis best explains how sound devices can contribute to poetic meaning?
options: Alliteration always creates happiness.
Harsh consonant clusters can reinforce a description of conflict when their effects are supported by the surrounding imagery and context.
Rhyme always indicates that a poem is humorous.
Sound patterns are unrelated to thematic development.
questions.answer: Harsh consonant clusters can reinforce a description of conflict when their effects are supported by the surrounding imagery and context.
questions.rationale: Sound effects depend on the interaction between language, context, imagery, and purpose.

questions.prompt: A poem repeatedly compares a difficult relationship to a garden that requires attention, pruning, and renewal. Which technique is most clearly developed?
options: Extended metaphor
End rhyme
Dramatic irony
Chronological exposition
questions.answer: Extended metaphor
questions.rationale: The sustained comparison develops through several related images.

questions.prompt: A speaker describes a city as a restless machine. What makes this expression a metaphor?
options: It presents the city in terms of another thing to suggest a meaningful relationship.
It identifies the city's exact population.
It uses the comparison word like.
It establishes a regular metrical pattern.
questions.answer: It presents the city in terms of another thing to suggest a meaningful relationship.
questions.rationale: The metaphor suggests qualities of the city through comparison with a machine.

questions.prompt: A poem presents an image of a locked door in several different contexts. Which approach provides the strongest symbolic interpretation?
options: Assume that every locked door symbolizes fear.
Consult a universal symbol dictionary and accept its first definition.
Examine how the door relates to the poem's speaker, recurring images, conflicts, and changes in meaning.
Ignore the door because it is an ordinary object.
questions.answer: Examine how the door relates to the poem's speaker, recurring images, conflicts, and changes in meaning.
questions.rationale: Symbolic meanings emerge from textual relationships and context rather than fixed universal definitions.

questions.prompt: A poem places an image of a lavish celebration immediately beside an image of a hungry child. Which technique most directly creates the relationship between these images?
options: Juxtaposition
Scansion
End rhyme
Apostrophe
questions.answer: Juxtaposition
questions.rationale: The placement of contrasting images near one another encourages readers to examine their relationship.

questions.prompt: A poem's speaker repeatedly praises a powerful ruler, but the descriptions reveal cruelty and injustice. Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: The poem necessarily endorses the ruler's actions.
The contrast may create irony that encourages readers to question the speaker's praise.
The poem contains no meaningful speaker.
The descriptions eliminate the possibility of a political theme.
questions.answer: The contrast may create irony that encourages readers to question the speaker's praise.
questions.rationale: The difference between explicit praise and implied criticism can create ironic meaning.

questions.prompt: Why should readers distinguish a poem's speaker from its poet?
options: Poets are never influenced by personal experience.
A poem may use a constructed voice whose beliefs, experiences, or attitudes differ from those of its author.
Every poem is written from an omniscient perspective.
The speaker's identity has no effect on interpretation.
questions.answer: A poem may use a constructed voice whose beliefs, experiences, or attitudes differ from those of its author.
questions.rationale: A poetic speaker is a textual voice and should not automatically be equated with the author.

questions.prompt: A poem begins with affectionate descriptions of a childhood home but gradually introduces images of decay and abandonment. Which interpretation best explains the shift?
options: The poem changes from lyric poetry to drama.
The changing imagery complicates the speaker's initial nostalgia and develops a more complex understanding of memory.
The poet abandons the poem's subject.
The poem no longer contains a consistent theme.
questions.answer: The changing imagery complicates the speaker's initial nostalgia and develops a more complex understanding of memory.
questions.rationale: Changes in imagery and tone can develop or complicate a poem's central ideas.

questions.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between tone and mood?
options: Tone describes the speaker's conveyed attitude, while mood describes the emotional atmosphere created for readers or listeners.
Tone and mood always refer to the poet's personal emotions.
Mood identifies a poem's rhyme scheme.
Tone refers exclusively to the volume of an oral performance.
questions.answer: Tone describes the speaker's conveyed attitude, while mood describes the emotional atmosphere created for readers or listeners.
questions.rationale: Tone and mood are related but distinct aspects of poetic experience.

questions.prompt: A sonnet spends its opening lines describing a problem and then shifts toward an unexpected reconsideration. Which term best describes the significant turn in thought?
options: Volta
Alliteration
Consonance
Enjambment
questions.answer: Volta
questions.rationale: A volta is a significant shift in thought, perspective, argument, or emotional direction.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes free verse?
options: Poetry without any deliberate structure
Poetry that must avoid every form of rhyme
Poetry without a fixed metrical or rhyme scheme that can still use purposeful rhythm, lineation, repetition, and other patterns
Poetry consisting only of complete prose sentences
questions.answer: Poetry without a fixed metrical or rhyme scheme that can still use purposeful rhythm, lineation, repetition, and other patterns
questions.rationale: Free verse permits flexible structural choices rather than eliminating structure.

questions.prompt: A poem repeats the same line after each stanza, but the line becomes increasingly ironic as new details emerge. What is the strongest explanation of the refrain's effect?
options: The refrain prevents thematic development.
The refrain creates structural continuity while acquiring new meaning through its changing context.
The refrain proves that the poem has only one interpretation.
The refrain functions only as a decorative sound device.
questions.answer: The refrain creates structural continuity while acquiring new meaning through its changing context.
questions.rationale: Repeated language can develop meaning as surrounding images, ideas, and circumstances change.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a defensible thematic interpretation rather than a topic?
options: Memory
A speaker describes a photograph.
The poem has four stanzas.
Memory can preserve emotional connections while also intensifying awareness of loss.
questions.answer: Memory can preserve emotional connections while also intensifying awareness of loss.
questions.rationale: The statement expresses a developed insight rather than naming a subject or describing a structural feature.

questions.prompt: Two poems address freedom. One uses images of flight, while the other uses images of open roads. Which comparative approach is strongest?
options: Assume the poems communicate identical themes because they share a subject.
Analyze how each image pattern develops a particular understanding of freedom and compare the resulting thematic meanings.
Determine which poem contains more lines and declare it more effective.
Ignore the images because both poems address the same topic.
questions.answer: Analyze how each image pattern develops a particular understanding of freedom and compare the resulting thematic meanings.
questions.rationale: Comparative analysis examines how different poetic choices develop related or contrasting meanings.

questions.prompt: A poem's final line can plausibly suggest both reconciliation and resignation. What should a reader do?
options: Assume that ambiguity is always a flaw.
Select whichever interpretation is more personally appealing without examining the text.
Evaluate the textual evidence supporting each interpretation and consider whether the ambiguity contributes to the poem's meaning.
Ignore the final line because it is difficult to interpret.
questions.answer: Evaluate the textual evidence supporting each interpretation and consider whether the ambiguity contributes to the poem's meaning.
questions.rationale: Purposeful ambiguity can support multiple defensible interpretations that should be evaluated through evidence.

questions.prompt: A performer pauses before a poem's final word and delivers it more quietly than the preceding lines. Which analysis best evaluates this choice?
options: The performer necessarily changes the poem's rhyme scheme.
The pause and reduced volume may emphasize the final word and create a reflective or intimate effect.
The performer eliminates the poem's imagery.
The performance proves that the poet intended only one possible meaning.
questions.answer: The pause and reduced volume may emphasize the final word and create a reflective or intimate effect.
questions.rationale: Delivery choices influence emphasis and audience experience without necessarily changing the written text.

questions.prompt: Which revision most effectively transforms the statement I felt lonely into concrete poetic imagery?
options: I felt very, very lonely.
Loneliness is an emotion that people experience.
Across the table, the second cup cooled untouched.
The speaker was experiencing loneliness.
questions.answer: Across the table, the second cup cooled untouched.
questions.rationale: The concrete image communicates absence through an observable detail rather than directly naming the emotion.

questions.prompt: A student wants to create a poem that gradually develops a sense of urgency. Which combination of techniques could most directly support that purpose?
options: Increasingly short lines, recurring imperatives, and accelerating rhythmic patterns
Randomly changing every word to a longer synonym
Removing every significant image
Using a fixed number of adjectives in each stanza regardless of meaning
questions.answer: Increasingly short lines, recurring imperatives, and accelerating rhythmic patterns
questions.rationale: Purposeful changes in structure, syntax, and rhythm can intensify urgency.

questions.prompt: A student writing a sonnet discovers that a required rhyme leads to an awkward phrase that weakens the intended meaning. Which response demonstrates the strongest craft judgment?
options: Keep the awkward phrase because rhyme is always more important than meaning.
Replace the phrase with unrelated words that happen to rhyme.
Reconsider the wording or rhyme pattern while preserving the intended meaning and making a purposeful decision about the form.
Remove every poetic technique from the composition.
questions.answer: Reconsider the wording or rhyme pattern while preserving the intended meaning and making a purposeful decision about the form.
questions.rationale: Poetic conventions should support meaning and purpose rather than force ineffective language.

questions.prompt: Which revision most directly strengthens thematic development in a poem about belonging?
options: Add the word belonging to the end of every line.
Develop a recurring image whose meaning changes as the speaker's understanding of community develops.
Replace all concrete nouns with abstract nouns.
Add a rhyme to every line without considering meaning.
questions.answer: Develop a recurring image whose meaning changes as the speaker's understanding of community develops.
questions.rationale: Thematic development emerges through meaningful relationships and changes across a poem.

questions.prompt: Which peer feedback comment provides the most useful evidence-based guidance for poetic revision?
options: I liked it.
Make it rhyme more.
The recurring window image creates a sense of separation, but the final stanza introduces an unrelated ocean metaphor that weakens the established pattern.
Poetry should always be longer.
questions.answer: The recurring window image creates a sense of separation, but the final stanza introduces an unrelated ocean metaphor that weakens the established pattern.
questions.rationale: The comment identifies a specific craft choice, explains its effect, and identifies a meaningful opportunity for revision.

questions.prompt: Explain how a poem's form can reinforce or complicate its content. Provide an example.
questions.answer: A successful response explains a relationship between structural design and meaning. For example, a villanelle's recurring refrains may reinforce a speaker's determination while also revealing an inability to escape a troubling thought.
questions.rationale: The task assesses understanding of the interaction between poetic form and content.

questions.prompt: Explain how enjambment can create temporary ambiguity or suspense.
questions.answer: A successful response explains that a grammatical unit continues beyond a line ending, allowing readers to encounter an incomplete or temporarily misleading meaning before the next line supplies additional information.
questions.rationale: Lineation can influence the timing and interpretation of poetic language.

questions.prompt: Explain how a poet might use caesura to contribute to meaning.
questions.answer: A poet might use an internal pause to emphasize hesitation, interruption, contrast, reflection, or a significant emotional shift. The response should explain the relationship between the pause and the poem's specific context.
questions.rationale: Students should evaluate structural techniques according to their effects rather than assign one universal meaning.

questions.prompt: Describe how an extended metaphor differs from an isolated metaphor.
questions.answer: An isolated metaphor establishes a figurative comparison at a particular moment. An extended metaphor develops the comparison through multiple related details, allowing its meaning to expand, change, or become more complex across a text.
questions.rationale: The task assesses understanding of figurative development across a poem.

questions.prompt: Explain why a poem's speaker may reveal information unintentionally.
questions.answer: A constructed speaker may express beliefs, assumptions, or attitudes that readers recognize as revealing aspects of character beyond the speaker's intended message. Contradictions, omissions, irony, and diction can create this effect.
questions.rationale: The task assesses understanding of poetic persona and implied meaning.

questions.prompt: Explain how the same refrain can acquire different meanings across a poem.
questions.answer: A refrain's words may remain unchanged while surrounding images, events, or ideas develop. Each recurrence can therefore reinforce, complicate, or challenge the reader's earlier interpretation of the repeated language.
questions.rationale: Repetition can create thematic progression rather than merely repeat information.

questions.prompt: Explain how a reader can use historical or cultural context without replacing close reading.
questions.answer: The reader should use relevant context to clarify references, conventions, circumstances, or possible implications while continuing to ground interpretations in the poem's actual language, structure, imagery, and other textual evidence.
questions.rationale: Context should deepen rather than substitute for literary analysis.

questions.prompt: Describe how two poems addressing the same subject can develop contrasting themes.
questions.answer: The poems may use different speakers, images, metaphors, forms, tones, or structural developments to communicate different insights about the shared subject. A successful response explains how those choices contribute to contrasting meanings.
questions.rationale: Shared subject matter does not establish identical thematic interpretation.

questions.prompt: Explain why a literary critique should involve more than a statement of personal enjoyment.
questions.answer: A critique evaluates artistic choices according to meaningful criteria such as coherence, thematic depth, precision, audience engagement, or effectiveness. It supports judgments with specific evidence and reasoning rather than relying only on preference.
questions.rationale: The standard requires evidence-based evaluation and critique.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways oral performance can influence the interpretation of a poem.
questions.answer: Possible responses include using pauses to emphasize structural shifts, changing tempo to influence urgency, varying volume to create contrast, using intonation to communicate attitude, or stressing particular words to highlight relationships among ideas.
questions.rationale: Poetic presentation includes meaningful choices beyond the printed text.

questions.prompt: Explain how a poet can create a purposeful structure in free verse without using a regular rhyme scheme.
questions.answer: A poet can organize free verse through recurring images, stanza patterns, line lengths, syntactic repetition, shifts in perspective, rhythm, white space, or thematic progression. These choices can create coherence and emphasis without fixed rhyme.
questions.rationale: Free verse depends on deliberate structural choices rather than an absence of organization.

questions.prompt: Describe how a writer might revise a poem to improve its imagery without making it unnecessarily longer.
questions.answer: The writer could replace vague descriptions with precise sensory details, remove redundant adjectives, select stronger verbs, develop a meaningful image pattern, and eliminate details that do not contribute to the poem's intended effect.
questions.rationale: Poetic revision emphasizes precision, compression, and purposeful language.

questions.prompt: Select a poem and evaluate how at least three poetic techniques work together to develop its meaning or theme. Use specific textual evidence and explain the relationships among the techniques.
questions.answer: A successful response establishes a defensible interpretation, identifies significant techniques, incorporates precise textual evidence, explains how the techniques interact, and develops a reasoned evaluation of their contribution to meaning or theme.
questions.rationale: The task directly assesses integrated evaluation of poetic techniques.

questions.prompt: Compare two poems addressing a related subject. Evaluate how differences in form, imagery, diction, sound, or perspective contribute to their distinctive thematic meanings.
questions.answer: A successful response establishes a meaningful basis for comparison, develops accurate interpretations of both poems, analyzes specific techniques, incorporates evidence from both texts, and evaluates the significance of similarities and differences.
questions.rationale: The task assesses comparative poetic interpretation and critique.

questions.prompt: Analyze a significant shift in a poem. Evaluate how the poet's structural and linguistic choices before and after the shift contribute to the poem's overall meaning.
questions.answer: A successful response identifies a defensible shift, analyzes relevant language and structural patterns on both sides of the shift, and explains how the change develops, complicates, or transforms the poem's meaning.
questions.rationale: The task assesses relationships among poetic structure, development, and thematic interpretation.

questions.prompt: Evaluate how a poem's fixed form supports or complicates its intended purpose. Consider the effects of rhyme, meter, repetition, stanza organization, or a significant structural turn.
questions.answer: A successful response accurately identifies relevant formal conventions, analyzes how the poet uses or adapts them, supports claims with textual evidence, and evaluates their contribution to the poem's intended effect.
questions.rationale: The task assesses evaluation of poetic conventions in relation to purpose.

questions.prompt: Compare a printed poem with an authorized oral performance of the same text. Evaluate how performance choices influence interpretation while considering the techniques present in the written poem.
questions.answer: A successful response distinguishes textual features from performance choices, analyzes specific examples of emphasis, pacing, pauses, or intonation, and evaluates how those choices influence meaning and audience experience.
questions.rationale: The task assesses interpretation of poetry across reading, listening, and viewing.

questions.prompt: Compose an original poem for a defined audience and purpose. Use a purposeful combination of imagery, figurative language, sound, and structural choices to develop an idea, emotional progression, or theme.
questions.answer: A successful poem demonstrates coherent development, precise language, purposeful imagery and figurative language, meaningful structural choices, and techniques that work together to support the intended purpose. The poem does not need to use every possible technique or follow a fixed form unless required by the selected task.
questions.rationale: The task directly assesses purposeful poetic construction.

questions.prompt: Create two poetic versions of the same central idea using contrasting forms or structural approaches. Explain how each version creates a different effect.
questions.answer: A successful submission presents two coherent poems or substantial poetic passages, demonstrates purposeful differences in form or structure, and explains how the choices influence emphasis, pacing, voice, meaning, or audience experience.
questions.rationale: The task assesses the ability to select and adapt poetic conventions according to purpose.

questions.prompt: Revise an original poem and submit a craft commentary explaining at least three meaningful changes involving diction, imagery, figurative language, sound, lineation, structure, or thematic development.
questions.answer: A successful submission demonstrates substantive revisions that strengthen the poem's intended effects and provides specific explanations connecting each revision to meaning, coherence, audience experience, or purpose.
questions.rationale: The task assesses reflective poetic decision-making and purposeful revision.

targets: I can identify an audience and purpose for my poem.
I can select a poetic form that supports my intended effect.
I can create a purposeful poetic speaker or voice.
I can use precise diction and sensory imagery to communicate an experience.
I can develop figurative comparisons that contribute to meaning.
I can use sound and rhythm to create emphasis or atmosphere.
I can use line breaks and stanza organization purposefully.
I can use repetition or recurring imagery to develop an idea across my poem.
I can follow or adapt poetic conventions to support my purpose.
I can create a coherent progression of ideas, images, or emotions.
I can revise my poem to strengthen precision, structure, sound, and thematic development.
I can explain how my poetic choices influence readers or listeners.
instruction: Begin composition by identifying an intended audience, purpose, subject, and desired effect.
Use mentor poems to demonstrate how different forms support different artistic purposes.
Provide opportunities to experiment with both free verse and fixed forms.
Teach students to distinguish the writer's identity from a constructed poetic speaker.
Model developing poetic voice through diction, syntax, perspective, and rhythm.
Use sensory observation exercises to develop precise concrete imagery.
Model transforming abstract statements into images that imply meaning.
Teach students to develop figurative comparisons through connected details.
Use extended metaphor planners to strengthen coherence across a poem.
Encourage purposeful use of symbolism and recurring imagery.
Model how rhythm and sound can influence the reader's experience.
Provide opportunities to read drafts aloud and evaluate their sound patterns.
Teach students to avoid forced rhyme and unnecessary metrical rigidity.
Use lineation experiments to demonstrate the effects of alternative line arrangements.
Model organizing stanzas according to developments in thought, imagery, or emotion.
Teach students to use punctuation and white space purposefully.
Demonstrate how refrains can acquire new significance as a poem develops.
Use mentor poems to examine purposeful structural and tonal shifts.
Encourage thematic development through imagery and relationships rather than explicit moralizing.
Provide short craft exercises before requiring longer or more complex poetic compositions.
Allow students to select forms and techniques appropriate to their purposes.
Provide alternatives to personal disclosure by allowing fictional speakers and observational subjects.
Use peer feedback protocols focused on intended effects and specific textual evidence.
Model substantial revision through changes in diction, imagery, sound, lineation, and structure.
Teach students to evaluate whether a poetic technique contributes meaningfully to the whole poem.
Provide optional performance opportunities with accessible alternatives.
Require craft commentaries explaining significant artistic decisions.
Assess poetic construction through criteria for purpose, precision, coherence, imagery, structure, thematic development, and purposeful technique.
evidence: A poetic planning document identifying audience, purpose, and intended effect.
A draft demonstrating a purposeful poetic speaker or persona.
An original poem using precise sensory imagery.
An original poem developing an extended metaphor or recurring image.
A composition demonstrating purposeful sound patterns or rhythm.
A poem using meaningful repetition or refrain.
A poem demonstrating purposeful lineation and stanza organization.
Two versions of a poetic passage using contrasting structural choices.
An original poem following the conventions of a selected fixed form.
An original poem deliberately adapting a poetic convention with a reasoned explanation.
A coherent free-verse poem demonstrating purposeful organization.
An original poem developing a meaningful idea, emotional progression, or theme.
A peer feedback response evaluating the effects of specific poetic choices.
A substantially revised poem demonstrating improved precision, coherence, or thematic development.
A craft commentary explaining how poetic techniques contribute to purpose and audience experience.
An optional original poetry performance demonstrating purposeful vocal delivery.
watchFor: Students beginning compositions without a clear purpose or intended effect.
Students assuming that poetry must rhyme or follow a fixed meter.
Students assuming that free verse requires no organization.
Students selecting a poetic form without considering its expressive possibilities.
Students forcing rhyme at the expense of precise or meaningful language.
Students treating poetic conventions as mandatory regardless of purpose.
Students creating a speaker without a consistent or purposeful perspective.
Students relying entirely on abstract statements rather than concrete imagery.
Students adding excessive adjectives instead of selecting precise details.
Students using figurative comparisons that are disconnected from the poem's central idea.
Students developing unrelated metaphors that weaken coherence.
Students repeating words or phrases without developing their significance.
Students arranging line breaks arbitrarily.
Students using stanza breaks without considering the progression of ideas.
Students including sound devices mechanically without considering their effects.
Students assuming that complex vocabulary automatically improves poetic quality.
Students attempting to include every available poetic technique.
Students presenting an explicit moral instead of developing meaning across the poem.
Students imitating mentor texts without developing an independent composition.
Students treating revision as spelling and punctuation correction only.
Students making revisions without considering the poem's intended audience or purpose.
Students evaluating their poems according to length or device count rather than effectiveness.
Students assuming public performance is necessary for every successful poetic composition.
Assessing students primarily according to performance confidence, conventional rhyme, or mechanical correctness rather than purposeful poetic craft.

unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are independently developed instructional recommendations rather than state-prescribed texts. Reading times are approximate instructional estimates and may include selected excerpts, rereading, or performance viewing. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Verify editions, translations, availability, copyright permissions, age suitability, and local instructional requirements before assigning materials. Public-domain status may vary by edition, translation, and jurisdiction. Some selections address war, death, racial oppression, grief, bullying, or other sensitive experiences and require thoughtful contextual preparation. Poetic forms and traditions should be taught with attention to their cultural and historical contexts. The instructional techniques listed throughout this card are recommended teaching content rather than an exhaustive list of separately mandated Georgia expectations.
